title: Introductory Economics
topics: Historical and cross-country growth, inequality, stability
Core concepts of micro and macroeconomics
Institutions as the rules of the game
Sources of market success and failure
Households and firms in the aggregate economy

notes.body:
For most of history GDP per capita was roughly flat. From around the 18th century in Britain, and later elsewhere, it turned sharply and persistently upward: the 'hockey stick'. This coincided with the capitalist revolution (private property, markets and firms becoming dominant) and a permanent technological revolution.

Key ideas
- Malthusian trap: with fixed land and diminishing average product of labour, higher income raises population until income falls back to subsistence. Technology produced more people, not lasting prosperity.
- Robert Allen's explanation of Britain's lead: high wages relative to cheap coal and capital made labour-saving machines profitable there first.
- Ratio (log) scale: equal vertical distances show equal proportional changes, so constant growth is a straight line.
- Divergence and catch-up: income gaps between rich and poor countries widened hugely after industrialisation. Some economies (Japan, South Korea, later China) caught up fast, but many did not.
- Stability: the golden age (early 1950s to early 1970s) ended in 1970s stagflation; the Great Moderation (mid-1980s to 2007) ended with the 2008 financial crisis.

Measuring inequality
- Lorenz curve: cumulative income share against cumulative population share, poorest first. The further below the 45° line, the more unequal.
- Gini coefficient: area between equality line and Lorenz curve ÷ total area under the equality line; 0 is perfect equality, 1 is maximal inequality.
- Kuznets (1955) suggested an inverted U as economies industrialise; rising top income shares since about 1980 challenge it as a general law. Piketty (2014) argues that when r > g, inherited wealth grows faster than income, so concentration tends to rise.

Worked examples
- Rule of 70: doubling time ≈ 70 ÷ growth rate (%). At 3.5% a year, about 20 years.
- Gini for incomes £10, £20, £30, £40: pairwise differences 10, 20, 30, 10, 20, 10 sum to 100, or 200 over ordered pairs. With n = 4 and mean £25, G = 200 ÷ (2 × 16 × 25) = 0.25. Doubling every income leaves G unchanged, because it measures relative inequality.
- Catch-up: A at $2,000 growing 6% and B at $8,000 growing 2% converge when (1.06/1.02)ᵗ = 4, so t = ln 4 ÷ (ln 1.06 − ln 1.02) ≈ 1.386 ÷ 0.0385 ≈ 36 years.

Exam pitfalls
- Using the rule of 70 with growth written as a decimal (0.035) instead of a percentage.
- Saying the world became more unequal without specifying between countries, within countries or globally across individuals.
- Treating proximate causes (capital, technology) as fundamental causes (institutions, geography, culture).

notes.h: Core concepts: scarcity, choice, efficiency and elasticity
notes.body:
Economics studies how people interact with each other and with the natural world in producing their livelihoods. CORE stresses that the economy is embedded in society, which is embedded in the biosphere.

Core concepts
- Opportunity cost: the value of the next best alternative forgone, not the sum of all alternatives.
- Reservation option: the next best alternative. Reservation price: the lowest price a seller accepts or the highest a buyer pays.
- Economic rent: a payment above what the reservation option would give.
- Pareto efficiency: no feasible change makes someone better off without making someone else worse off. There are many Pareto-efficient allocations, and the criterion says nothing about fairness. A Pareto improvement helps at least one person and harms nobody.
- Ceteris paribus: holding other variables constant to isolate one effect.
- Stocks (wealth, capital, debt) are measured at a point in time; flows (income, GDP, investment) per period. Real GDP uses constant prices; nominal GDP uses current prices.

Constrained choice
- MRS: the slope of the indifference curve, or how much of one good a person will give up for one more unit of another.
- MRT: the slope of the feasible frontier, or how much must be given up.
- At an interior optimum, MRS = MRT: the rate you are willing to trade equals the rate you are able to trade. With diminishing marginal product, the frontier is concave.

Elasticity
- Price elasticity ε = %ΔQ ÷ %ΔP. Demand is elastic if |ε| > 1, in which case a price rise lowers revenue.
- Midpoint formula: (ΔQ ÷ average Q) ÷ (ΔP ÷ average P), giving the same answer in either direction.
- Income elasticity is positive for normal goods, above 1 for luxuries and negative for inferior goods.

Worked examples
- Price rises from £10 to £12 and quantity falls from 100 to 80: %ΔQ = −20/90 = −22.2%, %ΔP = 2/11 = 18.2%, so ε ≈ −1.22. Revenue falls from £1,000 to £960.
- U = xy, income £80, px = £2, py = £4. MRS = y/x must equal 2/4, so x = 2y. Then 2(2y) + 4y = 80 gives y = 10 and x = 20, with £40 spent on each good.

Exam pitfalls
- Adding up all forgone alternatives for opportunity cost.
- Equating Pareto efficiency with fairness: a landowner capturing all the surplus can be efficient but unfair.
- Using simple percentage changes when the question asks for midpoint elasticity.
- Confusing MRS (preferences) with MRT (technology).

notes.h: Decision-making: game theory, social preferences and firms
notes.body:
Strategic interaction
- Nash equilibrium: each player's strategy is a best response to the others', so no one gains by deviating alone.
- Dominant strategy: best whatever others do.
- Prisoners' dilemma: defection is dominant for each, so mutual defection is the equilibrium, though mutual cooperation would make both better off. The equilibrium is Pareto inefficient.
- Coordination games have several equilibria; convention or history selects one.
- Repeated games: with enough weight on the future, tit-for-tat or grim trigger can sustain cooperation.

Social preferences and behaviour
- Ultimatum game: proposers often offer 40–50% and responders reject low offers, contradicting pure self-interest. This suggests fairness norms and reciprocity.
- Public goods game (Fehr and Gächter, 2000): contributions decline over rounds, but remain much higher when free riders can be punished.
- Present bias causes procrastination and under-saving. Sunk costs should be ignored, though people often do not.
- Borrowing and lending arise from diminishing marginal utility of consumption (a wish to smooth) plus impatience.
- Principal–agent problems arise when effort or behaviour cannot be contracted, as with workers and borrowers.

Firms that set prices
A firm maximises profit where MR = MC, equivalently where the isoprofit curve is tangent to the demand curve. The markup rule is (P − MC) ÷ P = 1 ÷ |ε|, so less elastic demand means a higher markup.

Worked examples
- MC = £30 and |ε| = 4: P = 30 ÷ (1 − 1/4) = £40, Lerner index 0.25. If a rival exits and |ε| = 2: P = £60, Lerner index 0.5.
- Monopoly with P = 100 − 2Q and MC = £20: MR = 100 − 4Q = 20 gives Q = 20, P = £60 and profit £800. Competitive output would be Q = 40, so there is a deadweight loss of ½ × 20 × 40 = £400.
- Fishing game with payoffs (3,3) for restraint, (5,0) for one overfishing and (1,1) for both: Overfish is dominant. Under grim trigger, restraint is sustainable if 3 ÷ (1 − δ) ≥ 5 + δ ÷ (1 − δ), which simplifies to δ ≥ 0.5.

Exam pitfalls
- Assuming a Nash equilibrium is efficient.
- Calling a strategy dominant when it is only a best response to one choice.
- Forgetting that the markup rule uses |ε| at the chosen point on the demand curve.
- Reading experimental generosity as pure altruism rather than as reciprocity or fear of rejection.

Goods markets
In competitive equilibrium supply equals demand among price-takers. Without externalities or information problems, all gains from trade are exhausted.
- Consumer surplus: the area under demand and above price. Deadweight loss: lost total surplus from blocked trades (monopoly, taxes).
- Tax incidence depends on elasticities, not on who legally pays. Consumers' share ≈ Es ÷ (Es + |Ed|).

Labour markets (CORE model)
- Labour discipline: the wage exceeds the reservation option, creating an employment rent. The threat of dismissal elicits effort. Cost of job loss ≈ rent per week × expected weeks unemployed.
- Efficiency wage: the firm minimises cost per unit of effort where the effort curve is tangent to a ray from the origin (the Solow condition).
- The wage-setting curve slopes up, since lower unemployment cuts the cost of job loss. The price-setting curve is flat at w/P = λ(1 − μ). Equilibrium always involves involuntary unemployment.
- Monopsony: a dominant employer pays below the marginal revenue product, so a moderate minimum wage can raise both pay and employment. Card and Krueger (1994) found no employment fall after New Jersey's minimum wage rise.

Credit markets
Lenders cannot observe effort or risk, so they ration credit rather than raise rates (Stiglitz and Weiss, 1981). Collateral and borrower equity give borrowers a stake, so people without wealth may be excluded. Present value: PV = X ÷ (1 + r)ᵗ.

Worked examples
- Demand Qd = 100 − 2P, supply Qs = 3P − 20: P = £24, Q = 52. With a £5 tax on sellers, consumers pay £27, producers get £22 and Q = 46. Revenue = £230 and deadweight loss = ½ × 5 × 6 = £15. At the old equilibrium Ed ≈ −0.92 and Es ≈ 1.38, so consumers bear about 1.38/2.31 ≈ 60%, matching the £3 rise.
- Pay £500 a week, effort disutility £100, benefit £200: rent = £200 a week; over 20 weeks unemployed, cost of job loss ≈ £4,000. Raising benefit to £250 cuts the rent to £150.
- Monopsony with supply w = 5 + 0.5L and MRP = 25 − 0.5L: the marginal cost of labour is 5 + L, so L ≈ 13.3 and w ≈ £11.67. The competitive outcome is L = 20, w = £15. A £15 minimum wage raises employment to 20.
- Credit: with success probability 0.9 if diligent and 0.6 if not, payoff £15,000 and effort cost £1,200, diligence requires 0.3(15,000 − R) ≥ 1,200, so R ≤ £11,000.

Exam pitfalls
- Assuming the legal payer bears a tax.
- Treating CORE unemployment as voluntary.
- Claiming minimum wages always cut employment.

notes.h: Institutions as the rules of the game
notes.body:
Douglass North defined institutions as the rules of the game in a society: formal rules (laws, constitutions, property rights, contracts) and informal ones (norms, conventions). Organisations such as firms are players under those rules.

Institutions and prosperity
- Acemoglu and Robinson (2012): inclusive institutions secure property and allow broad participation, encouraging investment. Extractive institutions channel income to elites.
- Acemoglu, Johnson and Robinson (2001) used settler mortality as an instrument. Where Europeans settled, they built protective institutions that raised long-run income.
- North and South Korea shared culture, geography and history before 1945 but diverged hugely under different institutions.
- North and Weingast (1989): after 1688, constraints on the Crown made its debt promises credible and cut borrowing costs.
- Rival explanations stress geography and culture; most economists see them as interacting with institutions.

Property, power and contracts
- Secure property rights (use, exclude, transfer) encourage investment because owners capture the returns. They also allow assets to be used as collateral.
- Bargaining power depends on reservation options and rules. Take-it-or-leave-it power lets one party capture all the rent; the outcome may still be Pareto efficient but very unequal.
- Incomplete contracts leave gaps (effort, quality) filled by power, monitoring and norms.
- Firms allocate by authority, markets by prices. Coase (1937) argued firms exist because markets have transaction costs.
- The state, in Weber's definition, claims a monopoly over legitimate force. It enforces rights but can be captured.
- Ostrom (Nobel 2009) showed communities governing common-pool resources sustainably through local rules, monitoring and graduated sanctions.

Coase theorem
With well-defined rights and low transaction costs, bargaining reaches an efficient outcome whoever holds the rights. The allocation of rights still determines who gains.

Worked example: smoke causes £300 a week of damage to a laundry, and a filter costs the factory £200. If the laundry has the right to clean air, the factory fits the filter (£200 < £300). If the factory has the right to pollute, the laundry pays it between £200 and £300 to fit the filter. Either way the filter is installed, but the factory is better off in the second case. In practice many victims, hidden information, enforcement costs and holdout break the result.

Exam pitfalls
- Confusing institutions (rules) with organisations (players).
- Claiming the Coase theorem says rights allocation does not matter: it matters for distribution.
- Treating formal land titling as automatically raising investment. Where informal tenure is already secure, or credit markets fail for other reasons, benefits may be small, so rigorous evaluation (for example randomised or staggered rollouts) is needed.

Why markets can work
- Adam Smith's invisible hand: self-interested exchange can, under conditions, promote the general good.
- First welfare theorem: with perfect competition, complete markets, no externalities and full information, competitive equilibrium is Pareto efficient.
- Hayek (1945): prices act as messages that summarise dispersed information.
- Schumpeterian innovation rents reward new technology and are competed away; rent-seeking preserves rents without creating value.

Sources of failure
- Externalities: negative ones lead to overproduction, positive ones to underproduction. A Pigouvian tax equals marginal external cost at the efficient output.
- Public goods (non-rival, non-excludable) are under-provided because of free riding. Common-pool resources (rival, non-excludable) are overused: the tragedy of the commons.
- Asymmetric information: adverse selection involves hidden characteristics before trade (Akerlof's lemons, 1970); moral hazard involves hidden actions after a contract. Both can create missing markets.
- Market power: a natural monopoly has economies of scale so large that one firm has the lowest cost, so it is often regulated.
- Second best (Lipsey and Lancaster, 1956): removing one distortion while others remain need not raise efficiency.
- Government failure: capture, poor information and political incentives mean intervention can make things worse.

Worked examples
- Demand P = 50 − Q, private MC = 10 + Q, external cost £6 per unit. The market gives Q = 20, P = £30. Social MC = 16 + Q, so the efficient output is Q = 17, P = £33. A £6 Pigouvian tax achieves this. Deadweight loss = ½ × 3 × 6 = £9.
- Abatement of 60 tonnes with MACA = 2a and MACB = 4b. A uniform 30-tonne cut costs a² + 2b² = 900 + 1,800 = £2,700. Cost-minimising abatement sets 2a = 4b with a + b = 60, so a = 40, b = 20 and cost = 1,600 + 800 = £2,400. A £80 tax gives the same split (2a = 80, 4b = 80), as would tradable permits trading at £80.
- Health insurance: adverse selection is countered by compulsory or pooled cover, and moral hazard by co-payments or excesses.

Exam pitfalls
- Defining public goods by who provides them.
- Mixing up adverse selection (before) and moral hazard (after).
- Treating market failure as sufficient for intervention: the costs of government failure must be weighed.
- Setting the Pigouvian tax equal to average rather than marginal external cost at the optimum.

Aggregate demand
AD = C + I + G + (X − M). Investment is far more volatile than consumption over the cycle. Firms postpone investment when expectations ('animal spirits') sour, while households try to smooth consumption.

Households
- Permanent income hypothesis (Friedman, 1957): consumption depends on expected long-run income, so temporary changes have small effects. Credit constraints, present bias and uncertainty limit smoothing.
- MPC: the share of extra disposable income spent. It is higher for credit-constrained households.
- Precautionary saving rises with uncertainty and depresses demand in downturns.
- Co-insurance, through family, insurance or the welfare state, helps smooth consumption.

The multiplier and the paradox of thrift
In a closed economy without taxes, the multiplier = 1 ÷ (1 − MPC). If investment also rises with output, the multiplier is larger. The paradox of thrift: if everyone tries to save more at once, income falls and total saving may not rise.

Labour market and output
Okun's law links rising unemployment to growth below trend; the coefficient varies across countries. Long-run living standards depend on labour productivity growth.

Finance and crises
- Bank leverage = assets ÷ equity. Banks are maturity transformers and vulnerable to runs (Diamond and Dybvig, 1983).
- Fisher's debt deflation (1933): falling prices raise real debt burdens, forcing spending cuts and asset sales. Recessions after banking crises tend to be deeper and longer (Reinhart and Rogoff, 2009).

Worked examples
- MPC 0.75 and investment falls by £20bn: the multiplier is 4, so output falls by £80bn.
- C = 50 + 0.75(Y − T), T = 100, G = 150, I = 10 + 0.1Y: Y = 135 + 0.85Y gives Y = 900 and private saving = 800 − 650 = 150. If autonomous consumption falls to 30, Y = 115 ÷ 0.15 ≈ 767 and saving ≈ 667 − 530 = 137. Saving falls: the paradox of thrift.
- A bank with assets £500bn and equity £25bn has leverage 20. A 5% default on £400bn of loans (£20bn) leaves equity of £5bn on assets of £480bn, so leverage is 96. Losses of £25bn (6.25% of loans) make it insolvent.
- Okun: Δu = −0.4(g − 2.5). With g = −2, unemployment rises by 1.8 points. To cut it by 1 point needs g = 5%.

Exam pitfalls
- Saying consumption is the most volatile component.
- Forgetting that induced investment enlarges the multiplier.
- Assuming that higher individual saving always raises aggregate saving.
- Using a leverage ratio of debt ÷ equity when assets ÷ equity is asked for.

Fiscal policy
- Automatic stabilisers respond without new decisions; discretionary policy faces recognition, decision and implementation lags.
- With lump-sum taxes, the spending multiplier is 1 ÷ (1 − c), the tax multiplier is −c ÷ (1 − c) and the balanced budget multiplier is 1. With proportional taxes and imports, k = 1 ÷ [1 − c(1 − t) + m].
- Crowding out weakens multipliers when higher borrowing raises interest rates, less so at the lower bound. Ricardian equivalence says forward-looking, unconstrained households save a debt-financed tax cut.
- Debt dynamics: Δd ≈ (r − g)d − pb. When r < g, the debt ratio can fall even with a small primary deficit.

Monetary policy
- Transmission: policy rate → market rates, asset prices, exchange rate and expectations → spending → inflation, with long and variable lags.
- Fisher equation: real rate ≈ nominal rate − expected inflation. Bond prices move inversely with yields; a perpetuity paying £C is worth C ÷ r.
- Taylor rule (1993): i = r* + π + 0.5(π − π*) + 0.5(output gap). Under the Taylor principle, rates rise more than one-for-one with inflation.
- At the effective lower bound, central banks use QE, buying bonds with new reserves; the Bank of England began in March 2009.
- Independence counters the inflation bias from time inconsistency (Kydland and Prescott, 1977). The Bank of England gained operational independence in 1997. The Chancellor sets the target, 2% CPI inflation.
- Phillips curve: a short-run trade-off that shifts with expectations (Friedman and Phelps). Inflation is stable at the NAIRU, where the wage-setting and price-setting curves meet.

Worked examples
- Taylor rule with r* = 2, π = 4, π* = 2 and a gap of −1: i = 2 + 4 + 1 − 0.5 = 6.5%.
- Nominal 5% and inflation 3%: the real rate is about 2%, or exactly 1.05 ÷ 1.03 − 1 ≈ 1.94%. A £5 perpetuity is worth £100 at 5%, £125 at 4%.
- With Y = 900, c = 0.75 and lump-sum taxes, closing a gap of 100 needs ΔG = 25, a tax cut of about 33.3, or a balanced rise of 100 in G and T.
- Debt 100% of GDP, r = 4%, g = 2%, primary deficit 1%: d′ = 1.04 ÷ 1.02 + 0.01 ≈ 1.030. Stabilising needs a primary surplus of about 1.96% of GDP. At r = 1%, d′ ≈ 1.000, and a 1% primary deficit roughly stabilises debt.

Exam pitfalls
- Stating the UK target as 2.5% (the old RPIX target, replaced in 2003).
- Forgetting that austerity can lower g and so worsen the debt ratio.

cards.b: Long-run GDP per capita was roughly flat for centuries, then turned sharply and persistently upward, first in Britain from around the 18th century and later in other economies at different dates.
The spread of private property, markets and firms as the dominant economic institutions. It coincided with the permanent technological revolution and the take-off in living standards.

With fixed land and a diminishing average product of labour, any rise in income leads to population growth until income falls back to subsistence. Technological progress therefore produces more people rather than permanently higher living standards.

cards.f: Why did the Industrial Revolution start in Britain? (Robert Allen's argument)
cards.b: In Britain, wages were high relative to the cost of energy (cheap coal) and capital, so labour-saving machines were profitable to adopt there first. Where labour was cheaper relative to energy, the same machines did not pay.
Doubling time in years ≈ 70 ÷ annual growth rate in per cent. At 2% a year income doubles in about 35 years; at 7% in about 10 years.

cards.f: Why plot GDP per capita on a ratio (log) scale?
cards.b: Equal vertical distances represent equal proportional changes, so a constant growth rate appears as a straight line. This lets you compare growth rates across countries with very different income levels.

Plots the cumulative share of income (or wealth) against the cumulative share of the population ranked from poorest to richest. The further it bows below the 45° line of perfect equality, the more unequal the distribution.

An inequality measure from 0 (complete equality) to 1 (one person has everything). Geometrically it is the area between the equality line and the Lorenz curve divided by the total area under the equality line.
Since the Industrial Revolution, income gaps between the richest and poorest countries widened enormously. Some economies (Japan, South Korea, later China) caught up rapidly, but many did not.

Simon Kuznets suggested that inequality first rises and then falls as an economy industrialises (an inverted U). The rise in top income shares in several rich countries since around 1980 casts doubt on it as a general law.

Roughly the early 1950s to the early 1970s, when advanced economies combined fast productivity growth, low unemployment and fairly stable inflation. It ended with the oil shocks and stagflation of the 1970s.
The period from the mid-1980s to 2007 when output and inflation volatility in many advanced economies was unusually low. It ended abruptly with the 2008 global financial crisis.
Piketty (2014) argues that when the return on capital (r) exceeds the growth rate of the economy (g), accumulated and inherited wealth grows faster than income, so wealth concentration tends to rise.
The value of the next best alternative given up when a choice is made.
A payment or benefit received above what a person would get from their next best alternative (their reservation option).
The reservation option is a person's next best alternative. The reservation price is the lowest price at which a seller will sell, or the highest price a buyer will pay.

An allocation is Pareto efficient if no feasible change could make someone better off without making someone else worse off. There are usually many Pareto-efficient allocations, and the criterion says nothing about fairness.
A change that makes at least one person better off and nobody worse off.
The amount of one good a person is willing to give up for one more unit of another while remaining equally well off. It is the slope of the indifference curve.
The amount of one good that must be given up to obtain one more unit of another. It is the slope of the feasible frontier.

cards.f: Condition for an interior optimal choice
cards.b: The indifference curve is tangent to the feasible frontier, so MRS = MRT: the rate at which you are willing to trade equals the rate at which you are able to trade.
Each additional unit of an input adds less output than the one before, holding the other inputs fixed.
'Other things equal'. A model isolates the effect of one variable by holding all other relevant variables constant.
Nominal GDP values output at current prices. Real GDP values it at constant prices, so it changes only when the quantities produced change.
A flow is measured per period of time (income, GDP, investment). A stock is measured at a point in time (wealth, capital, government debt).

cards.f: The economy as embedded in society and the biosphere
cards.b: In CORE's view the economy is part of society, which is part of the biosphere. Production draws on natural resources and generates wastes as well as goods.
% change in quantity demanded ÷ % change in price. Demand is elastic if |ε| > 1; then a price rise reduces total revenue.
% change in quantity demanded ÷ % change in income. It is positive for normal goods, above 1 for luxuries, and negative for inferior goods.
ε = (ΔQ ÷ average Q) ÷ (ΔP ÷ average P). Using averages gives the same answer whichever direction the price moves.
A set of strategies, one for each player, in which each strategy is a best response to the others. No player can gain by changing strategy on their own.
A strategy that gives a player a higher payoff than any alternative, whatever the other players do.

A game in which each player's dominant strategy is to defect, so the Nash equilibrium is mutual defection, even though mutual cooperation would make both better off (the equilibrium is Pareto inefficient).

A game with more than one Nash equilibrium (e.g. which side of the road to drive on), where players gain from choosing compatible strategies. History or convention often decides which equilibrium is reached.
Proposers typically offer a substantial share (often 40–50%), and responders often reject low offers, giving up money to punish unfairness. A purely self-interested model predicts neither.

cards.f: Public goods game with punishment (Fehr and Gächter, 2000)
cards.b: Without punishment, contributions decline over repeated rounds. When players can pay to punish free riders, contributions stay much higher, which suggests that reciprocity and norms can sustain cooperation.
Preferences about the wellbeing of others or about fairness (altruism, reciprocity, inequality aversion), held alongside concern for one's own payoff.
Putting disproportionate weight on immediate payoffs compared with later ones. It can cause procrastination and under-saving even when people plan to act otherwise.

cards.f: Why do people borrow and lend? (diminishing marginal utility of consumption)
cards.b: An extra pound of consumption is worth less when consumption is already high, so people prefer to smooth consumption over time. This, together with impatience (discounting), creates gains from borrowing and lending.
The combinations of price and quantity that give a firm the same profit. A profit-maximising price-setting firm chooses the point on its demand curve that reaches the highest isoprofit curve.
Produce where marginal revenue = marginal cost. For a price-setting firm this is where the slope of the demand curve equals the slope of the isoprofit curve.
(P − MC)/P = 1/|ε|, so a firm facing less elastic demand sets a higher markup. With |ε| = 5 the markup is 20% of price, so price is 25% above MC.

Arises when an agent's actions affect the principal's payoff but cannot be written into an enforceable contract because of hidden actions or information. Examples are worker effort and how a borrower uses a loan.
A cost already incurred that cannot be recovered. A rational decision ignores it, although people often do not (the sunk cost fallacy).

If a prisoners' dilemma is repeated indefinitely and players value the future enough, strategies such as tit-for-tat or grim trigger can sustain cooperation, because a defector loses future cooperative payoffs.

The price and quantity at which supply equals demand when all buyers and sellers are price-takers. All gains from trade are exhausted, so the allocation is Pareto efficient (if there are no externalities or information problems).
Buyers' willingness to pay minus the price actually paid, summed over all units bought. It is the area below the demand curve and above the price.
The loss of total surplus compared with the maximum achievable, caused for example by monopoly pricing or a tax that blocks mutually beneficial trades.
Who bears a tax depends on elasticities, not on who legally pays it. Consumers' share ≈ Es/(Es + |Ed|), so the less elastic side of the market bears more.
The employer pays a wage above the worker's reservation wage, so the worker gets an employment rent and the threat of dismissal elicits effort. Unemployment acts as a disciplining device.

cards.f: Employment rent and the cost of job loss
cards.b: Employment rent is the value of employment minus the reservation option (e.g. benefits), per period. The cost of job loss ≈ rent per week × expected weeks unemployed.

The firm sets the wage where the slope of the worker's best-response (effort) curve equals the slope of a ray from the origin, i.e. the marginal effort per pound equals average effort per pound. This minimises the cost per unit of effort.
The real wage needed to elicit effort at each level of employment. It slopes upward because lower unemployment reduces the cost of job loss, so firms must pay more.
The real wage consistent with firms' profit-maximising markup: w/P = λ(1 − μ), where λ is labour productivity and μ the markup as a share of price. It is horizontal in the employment rate.
Where the wage-setting and price-setting curves intersect. It always involves involuntary unemployment, because without unemployment there would be no cost of job loss to motivate effort.
A dominant employer faces an upward-sloping labour supply curve and pays below the marginal revenue product. A moderate minimum wage can then raise both pay and employment.
Compared fast-food employment in New Jersey, which raised its minimum wage, with neighbouring Pennsylvania. They found no fall in employment, which challenged the simple competitive prediction.
Lenders limit or refuse loans at the going interest rate rather than raising the rate, because higher rates attract riskier borrowers and weaken borrowers' incentives to make projects succeed.

cards.f: Role of collateral and borrower equity
cards.b: They reduce the lender's risk and give the borrower a stake in success, so wealthier borrowers get loans on better terms. People without wealth may be excluded from credit altogether.
PV = X/(1 + r)^t. For example, £110 received in one year is worth £100 today at r = 10%.
North described institutions as 'the rules of the game in a society': formal laws and informal norms that shape how people interact.
Formal institutions are written rules such as laws, constitutions, property rights and contracts. Informal institutions are social norms, conventions and codes of conduct.

Acemoglu and Robinson (2012): inclusive institutions protect property rights and allow broad participation, which encourages investment. Extractive institutions concentrate power and income in an elite and discourage growth.
Used historical settler mortality as an instrument for institutions. They argued that where Europeans settled in large numbers they built protective institutions that raised long-run income.

cards.f: North and South Korea as a natural experiment
cards.b: The two shared culture, geography and history before division after 1945 but adopted very different economic institutions. Their huge later divergence in living standards suggests that institutions matter.
Argued that the Glorious Revolution of 1688 constrained the Crown, which made its promises to repay debt credible and lowered the cost of government borrowing.
Legally protected rights to use an asset, exclude others from it and transfer it. Secure rights encourage investment because owners capture its returns.
The ability to capture a larger share of the economic rent from an interaction. It depends on each party's reservation option and on the rules governing the interaction.
A party who can set the terms can push the other to their reservation indifference curve and capture all the rent. The outcome can still be Pareto efficient, even though it is very unequal.
Elinor Ostrom (Nobel 2009) documented communities that manage common-pool resources sustainably through local rules, monitoring and graduated sanctions, without privatisation or state control.

If property rights are well defined and transaction costs are low, bargaining reaches an efficient outcome whoever initially holds the rights. The initial allocation of rights still affects the distribution of gains.
A contract that cannot specify or enforce everything that matters (e.g. worker effort, product quality). The gaps leave room for power, monitoring and norms to shape outcomes.

cards.f: Firms vs markets as allocation mechanisms (Coase, 1937)
cards.b: Inside a firm, resources are directed by managerial authority; in markets, by prices and voluntary exchange. Coase argued firms exist because using markets involves transaction costs.
A body that successfully claims a monopoly over the legitimate use of force in a territory. It enforces property rights and contracts, but it can also be captured by elites.
Adam Smith's idea that self-interested exchange in competitive markets can, under certain conditions, promote the general good without anyone intending it.

cards.f: First fundamental theorem of welfare economics
cards.b: Under perfect competition with complete markets, no externalities and full information, a competitive equilibrium is Pareto efficient.
A cost or benefit imposed on third parties that is not reflected in market prices. Negative externalities lead to overproduction; positive externalities lead to underproduction.
A tax per unit equal to the marginal external cost at the efficient output, so that private decision-makers take the external cost into account.
A good that is non-rival (one person's use does not reduce what is available to others) and non-excludable. Markets tend to under-provide it because people free ride.
A resource that is rival but non-excludable (e.g. a fishery). It is prone to overuse, which is the tragedy of the commons.
Hidden characteristics before a trade cause the quality of those choosing to trade to deteriorate. In Akerlof's (1970) market for lemons, high-quality sellers withdraw and the market can unravel.
Hidden actions after a contract is agreed: an insured or funded party takes less care because it does not bear the full cost of its actions.
A market that could create mutual gains fails to exist, often because of asymmetric information or contracts that cannot be enforced (e.g. insurance against some risks).
Market prices summarise dispersed information about scarcity and preferences, prompting buyers and sellers to respond without any central planner.

An industry in which economies of scale are so large that one firm can supply the whole market at lower average cost than two or more firms could. Such industries are often regulated or publicly owned.
Innovation rents (Schumpeter) are temporary profits from new technology that competition erodes. Rent-seeking uses lobbying or entry barriers to preserve rents without creating value.
Intervention that produces outcomes worse than the market would, for example through regulatory capture, poor information or political incentives.

cards.f: Theory of the second best (Lipsey and Lancaster, 1956)
cards.b: If one market distortion cannot be removed, removing another distortion does not necessarily raise efficiency. Policy must consider all the distortions together.
AD = C + I + G + (X − M): total spending on domestically produced goods and services.
Households prefer stable consumption, so they save in good times and borrow or run down savings in bad times. Credit constraints and weakness of will limit how far they can do this.
Consumption depends on expected long-run income, so temporary income changes have small effects on consumption and permanent changes have large ones.
The fraction of an extra pound of disposable income that is spent. Credit-constrained households tend to have higher MPCs.
Investment is far more volatile over the business cycle than household consumption, which is comparatively smooth.
A negative relationship between the change in the unemployment rate and output growth relative to trend. The size of the coefficient varies across countries and periods.
The total change in output caused by an autonomous change in spending. In a closed economy with no taxes it equals 1/(1 − MPC); an MPC of 0.8 gives 5.
If all households try to save more at the same time, aggregate demand and income fall, so total saving may not rise and can even fall.
Saving more when the future is uncertain, for instance from fear of job loss. It can depress aggregate demand during downturns.
Keynes's term for the confidence and expectations that drive investment decisions beyond calculable returns. They help explain why investment is volatile.
Pooling of risks by households, informally (family, community) or formally (insurance, the welfare state), to help smooth consumption.
Falling prices raise the real burden of debt. Borrowers then cut spending and sell assets, which pushes prices down further.

cards.f: Labour productivity and long-run living standards
cards.b: Labour productivity is output per hour worked. Long-run living standards depend chiefly on its growth, which comes from technology and capital accumulation.
Leverage is the ratio of total assets to equity. With leverage of 20, a 5% fall in asset values wipes out the bank's equity entirely.
Banks fund long-term, illiquid loans with short-term deposits. This makes them vulnerable to runs if depositors lose confidence (Diamond and Dybvig, 1983).
Taxes and transfers that respond to the cycle without new decisions: tax revenue falls and benefit spending rises in recessions, which dampens fluctuations.
Deliberate changes to government spending or tax rates to influence aggregate demand. It is subject to recognition, decision and implementation lags.

cards.f: Multiplier with proportional taxes and imports
cards.b: k = 1/[1 − c(1 − t) + m], where c is the MPC, t the tax rate and m the marginal propensity to import. With c = 0.8, t = 0.25 and m = 0.1, k = 2.
In the simple model with lump-sum taxes, raising G and T by the same amount raises output by exactly that amount, so the multiplier is 1.
Higher government borrowing may raise interest rates and reduce private investment, weakening the fiscal multiplier. It matters less when interest rates are stuck at the lower bound.
If households are forward-looking and not credit-constrained, they save all of a debt-financed tax cut to pay the future taxes it implies, so aggregate demand is unchanged.
Δd ≈ (r − g)d − pb, where d is debt/GDP, r the nominal interest rate, g nominal GDP growth and pb the primary balance. If r < g, the debt ratio can fall even with a small primary deficit.

A change in the policy rate passes to market and bank lending rates, asset prices, the exchange rate and expectations. These affect consumption and investment, and then output and inflation, with long and variable lags.
Real interest rate ≈ nominal interest rate − expected inflation.
i = r* + π + 0.5(π − π*) + 0.5(output gap). The policy rate rises more than one-for-one with inflation (the Taylor principle), so the real rate rises when inflation is above target.
Policy rates cannot go far below zero because people can hold cash instead. This limits conventional monetary policy in deep recessions.
The central bank creates reserves to buy assets, mainly government bonds, which lowers long-term yields when policy rates are near zero. The Bank of England began QE in March 2009.

Delegating monetary policy to an independent central bank with an inflation target improves credibility and counters the inflation bias identified by Kydland and Prescott (1977). The Bank of England gained operational independence in 1997.
The Bank of England's Monetary Policy Committee targets 2% CPI inflation. The target is set by the Chancellor.
A short-run inverse relationship between unemployment and inflation (Phillips, 1958). Friedman and Phelps argued that it shifts with inflation expectations, so there is no permanent trade-off.
They move inversely. A perpetuity paying £5 a year is worth £5/r: £100 when r = 5% and £125 when r = 4%.
The unemployment rate at which the wage-setting and price-setting curves intersect, so the bargaining gap is zero and inflation stays constant. Often called the NAIRU.

questions.q: Which statement best describes the 'hockey stick' pattern in long-run GDP per capita?
options: GDP per capita has grown at a steady rate since antiquity
GDP per capita was roughly flat for centuries, then rose sharply and persistently, starting in Britain from around the 18th century
GDP per capita rose rapidly in the Middle Ages and has been flat since the Industrial Revolution
GDP per capita rose at the same time and at the same rate in all countries after 1800
questions.why: Living standards were broadly stagnant for most of history. Sustained growth began with the Industrial Revolution in Britain and spread unevenly to other countries.

questions.q: A country's real GDP per capita grows at a constant 3.5% a year. Roughly how long will it take to double?
questions.why: By the rule of 70, doubling time ≈ 70 ÷ 3.5 = 20 years.

questions.q: Explain the Malthusian trap, and explain why Britain escaped it after the Industrial Revolution.
markScheme: Land is fixed, so the average product of labour diminishes as population rises
A rise in income (e.g. from a new technology) raises population growth
Population growth then lowers income per head back towards subsistence, so technology brings more people rather than richer people
Escape: after the Industrial Revolution, productivity growth was persistent and outpaced population growth (helped later by falling fertility), so incomes rose continuously
questions.modelAnswer: In Malthus's model land is fixed, so adding workers lowers the average product of labour. A technological improvement raises income above subsistence for a while, but higher income raises population, and the extra workers push income per head back down. Technology therefore produces a larger population at the same standard of living. Britain escaped because technological progress after the Industrial Revolution became continuous rather than one-off: productivity grew faster than population for generation after generation. Later, the demographic transition slowed population growth, and trade and fossil energy eased the constraint of fixed land.

questions.q: Four people have incomes of £10, £20, £30 and £40. Using G = (sum of |yi − yj| over all ordered pairs i, j) ÷ (2n² × mean income), calculate the Gini coefficient. What happens to the Gini if every income doubles? Explain.
markScheme: Sum of absolute differences over distinct pairs = 10+20+30+10+20+10 = 100, so 200 over all ordered pairs
Denominator: 2 × 16 × 25 = 800
Doubling every income leaves G unchanged at 0.25, because the Gini measures relative inequality (numerator and denominator both double)
questions.modelAnswer: The absolute differences between distinct pairs are 10, 20, 30, 10, 20 and 10, which sum to 100. Each pair appears twice among the ordered pairs, so the numerator is 200. With n = 4 and mean income £25, the denominator is 2 × 16 × 25 = 800. So G = 200/800 = 0.25, a fairly equal distribution. If every income doubles, all the differences double and so does the mean, so G stays at 0.25. The Gini is scale-invariant: it measures relative, not absolute, inequality.

questions.q: In 1950 country A has real GDP per capita of $2,000 and country B has $8,000 (constant prices). From 1950 onwards A grows at a steady 6% a year and B at 2% a year. (a) Using logarithms, calculate roughly the year in which A catches up with B, and check your answer using the rule of 70. (b) A's growth rate is similar to rates achieved by several East Asian economies during their catch-up periods. Explain why a poor country can grow this fast for a sustained period. (c) Evaluate why many poor countries did not converge on the rich in the second half of the twentieth century, distinguishing proximate from fundamental causes of growth.
markScheme: Rule-of-70 check: relative growth ≈ 3.9%, so the ratio doubles about every 18 years; two doublings ≈ 36 years
Catch-up: a poor country can adopt existing frontier technologies rather than invent them
Low capital per worker means high returns to investment before diminishing returns set in
Structural change from low-productivity agriculture to manufacturing, and export markets, add to growth
Convergence is conditional on saving, human capital, population growth and institutions
Fundamental causes: extractive institutions, insecure property rights, conflict and elite capture of rents
Other factors: commodity dependence, macroeconomic instability, geography and disease
Evaluation: catch-up growth slows as the frontier approaches, so 36 years is a lower bound; a stylised picture of convergence clubs rather than global convergence
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Catch-up requires 2,000(1.06)^t = 8,000(1.02)^t, so (1.06/1.02)^t = 4. Taking logs, t = ln 4/(ln 1.06 − ln 1.02) = 1.386/0.0385 ≈ 36 years, i.e. around 1986. As a check, A grows about 3.9% a year faster than B, so the ratio of their incomes doubles roughly every 70/3.9 ≈ 18 years. Closing a four-fold gap takes two doublings, about 36 years.

(b) A poor economy sits well inside the technological frontier, so it can grow by adopting technologies others have already developed, which is cheaper than inventing them. With little capital per worker, the marginal return to investment is high, so high saving and investment raise output strongly before diminishing returns set in. Moving labour from low-productivity farming into manufacturing raises average productivity further. Export-oriented manufacturing also gives access to large markets and a chance to learn by doing.

(c) The convergence prediction is conditional: it holds only among economies with similar saving, schooling, population growth and institutions. Capital and technology are proximate causes. The fundamental causes lie deeper. Where institutions were extractive, property rights insecure or politics unstable, investment and technology adoption were discouraged and elites captured the rents. Some countries depended on commodity exports with volatile prices. Others suffered debt crises and high inflation, especially in the 1980s, or had disadvantages of geography and disease. The stylised outcome is 'convergence clubs': rich economies and a group of fast-growing Asian economies converged, while much of sub-Saharan Africa and parts of Latin America fell further behind for long periods.

Evaluation: steady 6% growth is hard to sustain, because catch-up gains shrink as an economy nears the frontier. A would probably slow down before 1986, so 36 years is a lower bound on the time needed. The calculation shows how powerful compound growth differences are, but it is not a forecast.

questions.q: 'Economic growth since the Industrial Revolution has made the world both richer and more unequal.' Discuss, using historical and cross-country evidence.
markScheme: Defines the inequality concepts: between-country, within-country and global (across all individuals)
Richer: sustained per-capita growth, falling absolute poverty, higher life expectancy (stylised)
Between countries: large divergence from the 19th to the late 20th century
Recent decades: rapid growth in China, India and other Asian economies narrowed between-country gaps and reduced global inequality among individuals
Within countries: top income shares rose in the US and UK from around 1980; the trend is less marked in much of continental Europe and Japan
Kuznets inverted U and its limits; Piketty's r > g as an alternative account
Role of institutions and policy (taxation, unions, welfare states, golden age compression) shows that inequality is not determined by growth alone
Measurement issues: Gini vs top shares, income vs wealth, purchasing power adjustments
Evaluation: the statement is true for much of history but is a period-specific claim; growth is compatible with different distributions
Clear structure and a reasoned conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
The claim bundles two propositions, and its truth depends on which inequality is meant: between countries, within countries, or among all individuals in the world.

That the world became richer is clear. Before the Industrial Revolution, living standards were near subsistence almost everywhere. Sustained productivity growth then raised average incomes many times over in today's rich countries and, more recently, in large parts of Asia. The share of people in extreme poverty has fallen dramatically, and life expectancy has risen across the world.

On inequality between countries, the nineteenth and much of the twentieth century were an era of 'great divergence'. Growth began in Britain, Western Europe and its offshoots while much of the world stagnated, so the gap between richest and poorest widened enormously. Here the statement fits well. But since the late twentieth century, rapid growth in China, India and other Asian economies has narrowed between-country gaps, and most studies find that global inequality among individuals has fallen.

Within countries the picture is mixed. Top income shares fell in many rich countries for much of the mid-twentieth century and then rose sharply in the US and UK from about 1980, with smaller rises in much of continental Europe and Japan. This contradicts Kuznets's inverted U. Piketty's r > g mechanism offers one explanation; technology biased towards skilled workers, globalisation, weaker unions and lower top tax rates are others. The fact that countries at similar income levels differ so much shows that institutions and policy shape distribution: growth does not determine it.

Measurement matters too. Wealth is far more concentrated than income. Gini coefficients and top shares can move differently. Cross-country comparisons require purchasing-power adjustments.

Conclusion: growth made the world richer without qualification. It made the world more unequal for much of the industrial era, mainly through divergence between countries. That trend has partly reversed globally while within-country inequality has risen in some places. The relationship between growth and inequality is contingent on institutions, not a law.

questions.q: Aisha can attend a lecture, work a paid shift worth £40 to her, or go to the cinema, which she values at £25. She can only do one of the three. What is the opportunity cost of attending the lecture?
questions.why: Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative forgone, here the £40 shift. You do not add up every alternative.

questions.q: The price of a good rises from £10 to £12 and quantity demanded falls from 100 to 80. Using the midpoint method, what is the price elasticity of demand?
questions.why: %ΔQ = −20/90 = −22.2% and %ΔP = 2/11 = 18.2%, so ε ≈ −1.22. Demand is elastic, and revenue falls from £1,000 to £960.

questions.q: Distinguish Pareto efficiency from fairness, using an example.
markScheme: Definition: no one can be made better off without someone being made worse off
There are many Pareto-efficient allocations, including extremely unequal ones (e.g. one person has everything)
Fairness needs separate criteria (substantive judgements about outcomes, or procedural judgements about how they arose), so efficiency does not imply fairness
questions.modelAnswer: An allocation is Pareto efficient if nobody can be made better off without making someone else worse off. Many allocations meet this test. If a landowner uses take-it-or-leave-it power to pay a farmer only her reservation wage and keeps all the surplus, the outcome may be Pareto efficient, because no further gains from trade remain, yet most people would judge it unfair. Fairness requires separate criteria: substantive judgements about the outcome (such as equality) and procedural judgements about how it arose (free choice, equal opportunity).

questions.q: A consumer has utility U = xy, income £80, and faces prices px = £2 and py = £4. Using the condition MRS = price ratio, find the optimal bundle and interpret it.
markScheme: MRS = MUx/MUy = y/x
Set y/x = px/py = 1/2, so x = 2y
Substitute into the budget 2x + 4y = 80: 8y = 80, so y = 10 and x = 20
Interpretation: half of income goes on each good (£40 each); at the optimum the willingness to trade equals the market rate of exchange
questions.modelAnswer: With U = xy, MUx = y and MUy = x, so MRS = y/x. The optimum requires y/x = px/py = 2/4, so x = 2y. Substituting into the budget constraint 2x + 4y = 80 gives 4y + 4y = 80, so y = 10 and x = 20. The consumer spends £40 on each good. At this bundle the rate at which she is willing to swap y for x equals the rate at which the market lets her swap them, so no reallocation of spending can raise her utility.

questions.q: Sam is a self-employed farmer who can work h hours a day (0 ≤ h ≤ 24). Grain output is Y = 20√h and free time is t = 24 − h. Sam's preferences are U = t × Y. (a) Write down the MRT between free time and grain and Sam's MRS, and find the optimal hours of work, free time and output. (b) A new technology raises output to Y = 30√h. Find Sam's new choice and explain the result using income and substitution effects. (c) Over the twentieth century, average annual working hours fell substantially in rich countries while hourly productivity rose many times over. Keynes (1930) predicted a much shorter working week than actually emerged. Use your model to evaluate these facts.
markScheme: MRT = dY/dh = 10/√h (the slope of the feasible frontier in free time–grain space)
MRS = MUt/MUY = Y/t
Sets 20√h/(24 − h) = 10/√h, giving 20h = 240 − 10h, so h = 8
New technology: 30√h/(24 − h) = 15/√h, so h = 8 again; Y ≈ 84.9
Substitution effect: free time now has a higher opportunity cost, so Sam would work more
Income effect: Sam is richer and free time is a normal good, so he would work less; with these preferences the two effects exactly cancel
Historical evaluation: falling hours imply the income effect dominated in practice
Keynes's prediction failed because of rising consumption aspirations, status competition, institutions setting hours and inequality in who gained from growth
Limits: the model assumes free choice of hours, whereas employees often face hours set by employers, unions or law
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) The feasible frontier is Y = 20√(24 − t). Its slope (MRT) is dY/dh = 10/√h: the grain gained from one more hour of work. With U = tY, MRS = MUt/MUY = Y/t. The optimum requires Y/t = 10/√h, i.e. 20√h/(24 − h) = 10/√h. Multiplying out, 20h = 10(24 − h), so h = 8. Sam works 8 hours, takes 16 hours of free time and produces 20√8 ≈ 56.6 units.

(b) With Y = 30√h, MRT = 15/√h, and the condition becomes 30√h/(24 − h) = 15/√h, giving 30h = 15(24 − h), so h = 8 again. Output rises to about 84.9. Two forces offset each other. The substitution effect: each hour of free time now costs more grain, which pushes Sam to work more. The income effect: Sam can reach a higher indifference curve, and since free time is a normal good he wants more of it, which pushes him to work less. With these Cobb–Douglas preferences the effects cancel exactly, so all of the productivity gain is taken as consumption.

(c) Historically, hours fell as productivity rose, which in this framework means the income effect outweighed the substitution effect: societies took some of their growing prosperity as leisure. Yet hours fell by far less than Keynes expected. One reason is that preferences are not fixed. Consumption norms and status comparisons rise with average income, especially when inequality is high, so people may work to keep up with others. Another is that employees rarely choose their hours freely. Employers, unions and laws set standard working weeks, and the labour discipline model suggests firms prefer long hours from motivated workers. Cross-country differences in hours among similarly rich countries also point to institutions and policy, such as taxes and holiday entitlements, not just preferences.

Conclusion: the model clarifies the trade-off, but explaining real working hours requires social preferences and the institutions that govern work.

questions.q: A city council runs a museum that charges £10 entry and has 50,000 visitors a year. Researchers estimate the price elasticity of demand at the current price to be −0.4. The council proposes raising the price to £12 to boost revenue. The marginal cost of an extra visitor is approximately zero. (a) Estimate the new number of visitors and the change in ticket revenue. (b) Estimate the change in consumer surplus and in total surplus, treating demand as linear between the two points. (c) Evaluate whether the council should raise the price, considering the reliability of the elasticity estimate and wider economic arguments.
markScheme: %ΔP = +20%, so %ΔQ ≈ −0.4 × 20 = −8%: about 46,000 visitors
Revenue rises from £500,000 to £552,000 (+£52,000), as expected when demand is inelastic
Loss of consumer surplus ≈ £2 × 46,000 + ½ × £2 × 4,000 = £96,000
Change in total surplus with zero MC: −£44,000 (the £40,000 of lost revenue from deterred visitors plus a £4,000 triangle), i.e. a deadweight loss
Elasticity estimated at one point varies along the curve; long-run demand is likely more elastic
Distributional concerns: lower-income visitors are more likely to be priced out
Positive externalities and merit good arguments for low prices; alternatives such as price discrimination (concessions, tourist pricing)
A reasoned recommendation
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) A 20% price rise with ε = −0.4 implies roughly an 8% fall in visitors, from 50,000 to about 46,000. Revenue rises from £500,000 to 46,000 × £12 = £552,000, a gain of £52,000. Because demand is inelastic, the price effect outweighs the quantity effect.

(b) The 46,000 remaining visitors each pay £2 more, a transfer of £92,000. The 4,000 deterred visitors lose surplus of about ½ × £2 × 4,000 = £4,000. Consumer surplus therefore falls by about £96,000. With marginal cost near zero, the council's gain is the £52,000 extra revenue, so total surplus falls by about £44,000. That is a deadweight loss: 4,000 people valued a visit above its zero cost but no longer go.

(c) The revenue case relies on a point elasticity estimate. Elasticity changes along a linear demand curve and is likely to be larger in the long run as people find substitutes, so the visitor loss may be understated. The policy is also regressive if price-sensitive, lower-income residents are the ones deterred. Museums may generate positive externalities, such as education and tourist spending in local businesses, which a narrow surplus calculation omits and which strengthen the case for low prices. If the council needs revenue, price discrimination could raise it with less deadweight loss: higher prices for tourists or special exhibitions, with free or concession entry for residents and students.

Overall, the rise would raise revenue but reduce total welfare. It is justified only if the council values the revenue highly, for example because the alternative is distortionary taxation or closing the museum. A targeted pricing scheme would be better.

questions.q: Which statement about a one-shot prisoners' dilemma is correct?
options: Mutual cooperation is the unique Nash equilibrium
Each player has a dominant strategy to defect, and mutual defection leaves both worse off than mutual cooperation
There is no Nash equilibrium in pure strategies
The Nash equilibrium is Pareto efficient
questions.why: Defection is dominant for each player, so mutual defection is the Nash equilibrium, yet both would be better off cooperating. The equilibrium is Pareto inefficient.

questions.q: Two players each choose Left or Right. Payoffs (Row, Column) are: (Left, Left) = (3, 2); (Left, Right) = (0, 0); (Right, Left) = (0, 0); (Right, Right) = (2, 3). Which are the pure-strategy Nash equilibria?
questions.why: At (Left, Left) and (Right, Right) neither player gains by deviating, because deviating gives 0. This is a coordination game with a conflict over which equilibrium is chosen.

questions.q: Explain how evidence from the ultimatum game challenges the assumption that economic actors are purely self-interested.
markScheme: Prediction under pure self-interest: the proposer offers the smallest possible amount and the responder accepts anything positive
Evidence: proposers commonly offer large shares (often 40–50%), and low offers are frequently rejected
Interpretation: responders sacrifice money to punish unfairness (reciprocity, inequality aversion), and proposers anticipate this or care about fairness
Behaviour varies across societies (cross-cultural studies by Henrich and co-authors), suggesting norms shape preferences
questions.modelAnswer: If both players care only about their own money, the proposer should offer the smallest possible positive amount and the responder should accept, since something beats nothing. Experiments contradict both predictions. Typical offers are large, often 40–50% of the pie, and responders frequently reject low offers, choosing zero for both rather than accept an unfair split. This suggests social preferences such as reciprocity and inequality aversion. Proposers may be fair-minded or may anticipate rejection. Cross-cultural studies find that offers vary between societies, which implies that social norms shape these preferences.

questions.q: A firm has constant marginal cost of £30 and, at its profit-maximising price, faces a price elasticity of demand of −4. (a) Calculate its price and Lerner index. (b) A rival exits and the firm's elasticity falls to −2. Calculate the new price and Lerner index and explain the intuition.
markScheme: Uses the markup rule (P − MC)/P = 1/|ε|, i.e. P = MC/(1 − 1/|ε|)
Lerner index = (40 − 30)/40 = 0.25
With |ε| = 2: P = 30/0.5 = £60 and Lerner index = 0.5
Intuition: with fewer substitutes, customers are less responsive to price, so the firm gains more by raising price than it loses in sales; market power rises
questions.modelAnswer: The profit-maximising markup satisfies (P − MC)/P = 1/|ε|, so P = MC/(1 − 1/|ε|). With |ε| = 4, P = 30/0.75 = £40 and the Lerner index is 10/40 = 0.25. After the rival exits, |ε| = 2, so P = 30/0.5 = £60 and the Lerner index is 0.5. With fewer close substitutes, customers respond less to a price rise, so the revenue gained on remaining sales outweighs the sales lost. The firm's market power, and the gap between price and marginal cost, both increase.

questions.q: Two fishing villages, Northport and Southport, share a lake. Each season each village chooses to Restrain or Overfish. Payoffs (Northport, Southport): both Restrain (3, 3); Northport Overfishes and Southport Restrains (5, 0); Northport Restrains and Southport Overfishes (0, 5); both Overfish (1, 1). (a) Identify any dominant strategies and the Nash equilibrium of the one-season game, and comment on its efficiency. (b) Suppose the game is repeated indefinitely and each village discounts future payoffs by a factor δ per season. Both use a 'grim trigger' strategy: restrain until the other overfishes, then overfish forever. Find the minimum δ for which restraint can be sustained. (c) Evaluate other ways the villages might sustain cooperation, drawing on experimental and field evidence.
markScheme: Overfish is dominant for each village (5 > 3 and 1 > 0)
Nash equilibrium (Overfish, Overfish) with payoffs (1, 1), which is Pareto inferior to (3, 3): a prisoners' dilemma and tragedy of the commons
Value of cooperating forever: 3/(1 − δ)
Value of deviating: 5 + δ × 1/(1 − δ)
Condition 3/(1 − δ) ≥ 5 + δ/(1 − δ) gives 3 ≥ 5 − 4δ, so δ ≥ 0.5
Interpretation: cooperation needs patience or a high probability that the interaction continues
Social preferences and reciprocity; public goods experiments with punishment (Fehr and Gächter) show peer punishment sustains contributions
Ostrom: local rules, monitoring, graduated sanctions and conflict resolution in real commons
Alternative institutions: quotas, property rights or tradable permits, regulation; their costs and enforcement problems
Evaluation of which approach suits two small villages, and a conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Whatever Southport does, Northport gains by overfishing: 5 > 3 if Southport restrains and 1 > 0 if it overfishes. The game is symmetric, so Overfish is dominant for both, and the unique Nash equilibrium is (Overfish, Overfish) with payoffs (1, 1). Both would prefer (3, 3), so the equilibrium is Pareto inefficient: a prisoners' dilemma, and a version of the tragedy of the commons.

(b) Under grim trigger, restraining forever yields 3 + 3δ + 3δ² + … = 3/(1 − δ). Deviating yields 5 today and then 1 in every later season: 5 + δ/(1 − δ). Restraint is sustainable if 3/(1 − δ) ≥ 5 + δ/(1 − δ). Multiplying by (1 − δ) gives 3 ≥ 5(1 − δ) + δ = 5 − 4δ, so δ ≥ 0.5. Villages that value the future enough, or expect to keep interacting, can cooperate without outside enforcement. Impatient villages, or those expecting the lake to be depleted soon, cannot.

(c) Repetition is not the only route. Experiments show many people have social preferences: in public goods games, contributions decay without punishment but stay high when participants can pay to punish free riders (Fehr and Gächter, 2000). Ostrom's field studies found communities managing fisheries, forests and irrigation for generations through clear boundaries, rules made by users, monitoring, graduated sanctions and cheap ways of resolving conflicts. For two neighbouring villages that know each other, monitoring is relatively easy, so a community agreement is plausible. External solutions include assigning property rights, setting quotas enforced by a regulator or creating tradable fishing rights. These need state capacity and accurate information, and they may crowd out existing norms of cooperation.

Conclusion: the one-shot model predicts overfishing, but repetition, social preferences and well-designed local institutions often prevent it. Policy should build on local norms rather than assume pure self-interest.

questions.q: A monopolist faces inverse demand P = 100 − 2Q and has constant marginal and average cost of £20. (a) Find the profit-maximising quantity, price and profit. (b) Calculate consumer surplus, and the deadweight loss compared with the competitive outcome where P = MC. (c) Calculate the price elasticity of demand at the monopoly optimum and show that the markup rule holds. (d) Discuss whether the deadweight loss would remain if the firm could perfectly price discriminate, and what this implies for the efficiency–fairness distinction.
markScheme: TR = 100Q − 2Q², so MR = 100 − 4Q
MR = MC gives Q = 20 and P = £60
Consumer surplus = ½ × 20 × (100 − 60) = £400
Competitive outcome: Q = 40 at P = 20; deadweight loss = ½ × (60 − 20) × (40 − 20) = £400
Perfect price discrimination: output rises to 40, there is no deadweight loss, and the firm captures all surplus (£1,600)
Evaluation: the outcome is Pareto efficient but consumers get nothing, so efficiency and fairness can diverge; implications for competition policy
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Total revenue is 100Q − 2Q², so MR = 100 − 4Q. Setting MR = MC = 20 gives Q = 20 and, from demand, P = 100 − 40 = £60. Profit = (60 − 20) × 20 = £800.

(b) Consumer surplus is the triangle between the demand intercept (£100) and the price: ½ × 20 × 40 = £400. Under competition, P = MC = 20, so Q = 40 and consumer surplus would be ½ × 40 × 80 = £1,600. Total surplus under monopoly is £400 + £800 = £1,200, so the deadweight loss is £400, the triangle ½ × (60 − 20) × (40 − 20). It represents units that consumers value above their cost but that are not produced because the monopolist restricts output to keep price high.

(c) From Q = 50 − 0.5P, dQ/dP = −0.5, so at the optimum ε = −0.5 × 60/20 = −1.5. The Lerner index is (60 − 20)/60 = 2/3, which equals 1/|ε| = 1/1.5, confirming the markup rule. A monopolist always operates on the elastic part of demand, because MR is negative where demand is inelastic.

(d) With perfect price discrimination, each buyer pays their full willingness to pay. The firm no longer has to cut the price on earlier units to sell more, so marginal revenue equals the demand curve and it produces until P = MC, at Q = 40. The deadweight loss disappears, but the firm captures the entire £1,600 of surplus and consumers get nothing. The outcome is Pareto efficient yet highly unequal. This illustrates that efficiency and fairness are separate criteria. Competition policy usually cares about consumer welfare, not just total surplus, and perfect discrimination is rarely feasible anyway because firms lack the information and resale is hard to prevent.

questions.q: Two firms, Alpha and Beta, sell an identical product and choose quantities simultaneously (Cournot competition). Inverse market demand is P = 120 − Q, where Q = qA + qB, and each firm has constant marginal cost of £12 and no fixed costs. (a) Derive each firm's best-response function and find the Nash equilibrium quantities, price and profits. (b) If the firms formed a cartel and split the monopoly output equally, what would each produce and earn? (c) Show that the cartel is not a Nash equilibrium by calculating Alpha's best deviation and its profit. (d) Using your results, evaluate why cartels form, why they tend to be unstable, and how competition authorities can exploit this instability.
markScheme: Alpha's profit (120 − qA − qB − 12)qA; first-order condition gives qA = (108 − qB)/2, and symmetrically for Beta
Nash equilibrium qA = qB = 36, Q = 72, P = £48
Monopoly: MR = 120 − 2Q = 12, so Q = 54 and P = £66; joint profit £2,916, so £1,458 each from 27 units
Deviation: best response to qB = 27 is qA = 40.5; P = 52.5; Alpha's profit = 40.5 × 40.5 = £1,640.25 > £1,458, while Beta's falls to £1,093.50
Hence collusion is not a Nash equilibrium: each firm has an incentive to cheat, like a prisoners' dilemma
Comparison with competition (P = 12, Q = 108): Cournot lies between monopoly and competition
Cartel stability with repeated interaction: patience, few firms, transparent prices and frequent interaction help collusion
Policy: leniency programmes exploit the incentive to defect, alongside fines and criminal sanctions; screening markets for signs of collusion
Evaluation and clear structure
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Alpha's profit is πA = (120 − qA − qB)qA − 12qA. Setting dπA/dqA = 108 − 2qA − qB = 0 gives the best response qA = (108 − qB)/2. By symmetry, qB = (108 − qA)/2. Solving together, qA = qB = 36, so Q = 72 and P = £48. Each firm earns (48 − 12) × 36 = £1,296.

(b) A monopolist would set MR = 120 − 2Q = 12, giving Q = 54 and P = £66, with profit (66 − 12) × 54 = £2,916. Split equally, each firm produces 27 units and earns £1,458, more than under Cournot.

(c) If Beta keeps to 27, Alpha's best response is qA = (108 − 27)/2 = 40.5. Total output becomes 67.5 and the price falls to £52.50. Alpha earns (52.5 − 12) × 40.5 = £1,640.25, while Beta's profit falls to 40.5 × 27 = £1,093.50. Because 27 is not a best response to 27, the cartel is not a Nash equilibrium. Each firm gains by expanding output when the other restricts, so the structure resembles a prisoners' dilemma. If both cheat, they slide back towards the Cournot outcome.

(d) The competitive benchmark (P = MC = 12, Q = 108) shows Cournot lies between monopoly and perfect competition. That gap is the gain from collusion that motivates cartels. Collusion is easier to sustain when the game is repeated and firms are patient, when there are few firms, when prices and outputs are observable so cheating is detected quickly, and when demand is stable. It breaks down when firms are numerous, products differ, or demand shocks make cheating hard to distinguish from bad luck.

Competition authorities exploit the instability. Leniency programmes, such as those run by the UK's CMA and the European Commission, offer immunity or reduced fines to the first cartel member to confess. This creates a new prisoners' dilemma among the colluders: each fears another will report first. Combined with heavy fines and, in the UK, the possibility of criminal prosecution of individuals, leniency raises the expected cost of collusion. Some cartels persist for years nonetheless, so authorities also screen markets for suspicious price patterns.

Conclusion: the static model explains why collusion is tempting and fragile; repeated-game reasoning explains why some cartels survive, and good policy design works on both.

questions.q: Consumer surplus in a market is best described as:
options: The total amount consumers spend on a good
The difference between buyers' willingness to pay and the price they pay, summed over all units bought
The difference between price and marginal cost
The revenue firms earn above their costs
questions.why: Consumer surplus is the area below the demand curve and above the price. Revenue above costs is producer surplus or profit.

questions.q: At the market equilibrium, the price elasticity of demand is −0.5 and the price elasticity of supply is 1.5. The government imposes a tax of £4 per unit on sellers. Approximately how much does the price paid by consumers rise?
questions.why: Consumers' share ≈ Es/(Es + |Ed|) = 1.5/2 = 0.75, so they bear about £3. The less elastic side of the market bears more of the tax, whoever legally pays it.

questions.q: Explain why, in the CORE model of the labour market, equilibrium always involves involuntary unemployment.
markScheme: The wage-setting curve gives the real wage needed to elicit effort at each employment level and slopes upward
The price-setting curve gives the real wage consistent with firms' markups and is horizontal
Equilibrium is at their intersection, where workers and firms are both doing the best they can
At full employment the cost of job loss would be zero, so no wage would elicit effort; unemployment is therefore an equilibrium feature, not a temporary disequilibrium
questions.modelAnswer: Firms pay wages above workers' reservation option so that losing the job is costly. The wage-setting curve shows the real wage needed to elicit effort at each employment rate. It slopes upward and becomes very steep near full employment, because a sacked worker would quickly find another job. The price-setting curve shows the real wage that firms' profit-maximising markup leaves for workers. Equilibrium is where the two curves meet. It must be below full employment, because with no unemployment there is no cost of job loss and no wage would motivate effort. Unemployed workers would like jobs at the going wage, so the unemployment is involuntary.

questions.q: A worker earns £500 a week and values the disutility of the effort the job requires at £100 a week. If fired, she would receive unemployment benefit of £200 a week and expects to be unemployed for 20 weeks. (a) Calculate her weekly employment rent and her cost of job loss. (b) Explain the effect of raising benefit to £250 a week.
markScheme: Weekly employment rent = (500 − 100) − 200 = £200
Cost of job loss = £200 × 20 weeks = £4,000 (ignoring discounting)
With benefit of £250: rent = £150 a week and cost of job loss = £3,000
A lower cost of job loss means less effort at the given wage, so firms must pay more for the same effort: the wage-setting curve shifts up
questions.modelAnswer: Net of effort, the job is worth £500 − £100 = £400 a week against £200 on benefit, so her employment rent is £200 a week. Over an expected 20-week spell, the cost of losing the job is about £4,000. If benefit rises to £250, the rent falls to £150 a week and the cost of job loss to £3,000. Since effort depends on how much the worker stands to lose, she will supply less effort at the same wage. Firms must raise wages to restore effort, so the wage-setting curve shifts up, which in the CORE model raises equilibrium unemployment, other things equal.

questions.q: In a competitive market, demand is Qd = 100 − 2P and supply is Qs = 3P − 20, where P is in pounds. (a) Find the equilibrium price and quantity. (b) The government imposes a tax of £5 per unit, paid by sellers. Find the new price paid by consumers, the price received by producers and the quantity traded. (c) Calculate the tax revenue and the deadweight loss. (d) Calculate the price elasticities of demand and supply at the original equilibrium and use them to explain the incidence you found. Briefly evaluate when such a tax might nonetheless be desirable.
markScheme: 100 − 2P = 3P − 20 gives P = £24 and Q = 52
With the tax, supply becomes Qs = 3(P − 5) − 20 = 3P − 35; solving gives P = £27 for consumers and Q = 46
Producers receive £22: consumers bear £3 (60%) and producers £2 (40%)
Revenue = 5 × 46 = £230
Deadweight loss = ½ × 5 × (52 − 46) = £15
Consumers' share = Es/(Es + |Ed|) = 0.6: demand is less elastic, so consumers bear more
Evaluation: the tax may be desirable if it corrects a negative externality (Pigouvian) or raises revenue at lower deadweight loss than alternatives
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Setting 100 − 2P = 3P − 20 gives 5P = 120, so P = £24 and Q = 52.

(b) The tax means producers receive P − 5 when consumers pay P, so supply becomes Qs = 3(P − 5) − 20 = 3P − 35. Setting 100 − 2P = 3P − 35 gives P = £27 and Q = 46. Producers receive £27 − £5 = £22. Consumers pay £3 more and producers receive £2 less, so consumers bear 60% of the tax although sellers legally pay it.

(c) Revenue is £5 × 46 = £230. The deadweight loss is the triangle of lost trades: ½ × £5 × (52 − 46) = £15. These six units were worth more to buyers than they cost to produce, but the tax wedge prevents them being traded.

(d) At the original equilibrium, Ed = (dQ/dP)(P/Q) = −2 × 24/52 ≈ −0.92 and Es = 3 × 24/52 ≈ 1.38. The incidence formula gives the consumers' share as Es/(Es + |Ed|) = 1.38/2.31 = 0.6, matching part (b). Buyers are less able to switch away than sellers, so the price they pay absorbs more of the tax. With linear curves, the ratio of the slopes, 3/(3 + 2), gives the same result.

Evaluation: the deadweight loss is small relative to revenue (£15 against £230) because demand is fairly inelastic and the tax is small relative to the price, so this would be a relatively efficient source of revenue. If the good generates a negative externality, the tax may raise total welfare by moving output towards the social optimum, in which case the 'deadweight loss' is partly offset or reversed. Distributional effects matter too: if the good is a necessity bought by poorer households, the tax may be regressive.

questions.q: Priya has a business project that costs £10,000 and pays £15,000 in a year if it succeeds and nothing if it fails. If she works hard, the probability of success is 0.9; if she does not, it is 0.6. Hard work costs her the equivalent of £1,200. Hard work cannot be observed or written into a contract.
