A bank can lend at an opportunity cost of 5%, and Priya repays an amount R only if the project succeeds (limited liability). (a) Find the condition on R under which Priya chooses to work hard. (b) Show that if Priya has no wealth, the bank will not lend to her, even though the project is socially worthwhile. (c) Suppose instead Priya has £4,000 of her own to invest and borrows only £6,000. Show that lending is now feasible. (d) Use your results to explain credit rationing and credit market exclusion, and evaluate policy responses.
markScheme: Effort is worthwhile for Priya if 0.9(15,000 − R) − 1,200 ≥ 0.6(15,000 − R)
This simplifies to 0.3(15,000 − R) ≥ 1,200, so R ≤ £11,000
Without wealth: the bank breaks even with a hard-working borrower if 0.9R ≥ 10,500, so R ≥ £11,667 > £11,000: no repayment satisfies both conditions
If Priya does not work hard, the bank needs 0.6R ≥ 10,500, so R ≥ £17,500 > £15,000: impossible
The project is socially worthwhile: expected value with effort 13,500 − 1,200 = £12,300 > £10,500 opportunity cost
With £4,000 equity: the bank needs 0.9R ≥ 6,300, so R ≥ £7,000 ≤ £11,000: feasible; Priya's expected payoff 0.9 × 8,000 − 1,200 = £6,000 > £4,200 from saving
Explains that raising the interest rate destroys incentives, so lenders ration credit rather than raise rates (Stiglitz and Weiss)
Wealth works like collateral: the poor are excluded, which entrenches inequality
Policy evaluation: public loan guarantees, microfinance with group lending, development banks; risks of moral hazard and fiscal cost
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Priya keeps 15,000 − R if the project succeeds. Working hard is worthwhile if 0.9(15,000 − R) − 1,200 ≥ 0.6(15,000 − R), i.e. 0.3(15,000 − R) ≥ 1,200, so 15,000 − R ≥ 4,000 and R ≤ £11,000. The more she must repay, the smaller her stake in success, and above £11,000 she stops working hard.

(b) To cover its opportunity cost of £10,500 when Priya works hard, the bank needs 0.9R ≥ 10,500, so R ≥ £11,667. That exceeds the £11,000 maximum consistent with hard work. If it expects her not to work hard, it needs 0.6R ≥ 10,500, so R ≥ £17,500, more than the project can ever repay. No contract works, so the bank refuses to lend. Yet with hard work the project's expected value is 0.9 × 15,000 − 1,200 = £12,300, more than its £10,500 opportunity cost. A socially worthwhile project goes unfunded.

(c) With £4,000 of her own money invested, the bank lends £6,000 and needs 0.9R ≥ 6,300, so R ≥ £7,000. Her incentive condition is unchanged (R ≤ £11,000) because her own stake is committed either way, so any R between £7,000 and £11,000 works. At R = £7,000 her expected payoff is 0.9 × 8,000 − 1,200 = £6,000, more than the £4,200 she would get by saving her £4,000 at 5%, so she goes ahead.

(d) Because hard work cannot be contracted, the interest rate does two jobs: it is the price of the loan, and it affects the borrower's incentives. Raising it beyond a point lowers the lender's expected return, so lenders ration credit instead of letting the rate clear the market (Stiglitz and Weiss, 1981). Wealth acts like collateral, so identical projects are funded for the rich and not for the poor. Credit markets can therefore entrench inequality and waste productive opportunities. Policy options include government loan guarantees, development banks and microfinance with group liability, where peers monitor one another. These can expand access, but guarantees can weaken lenders' screening and create fiscal costs, so their design matters.

questions.q: A town's only large employer faces the labour supply curve w = 5 + 0.5L, where w is the hourly wage in pounds and L is employment in hundreds of workers. The marginal revenue product of labour is MRP = 25 − 0.5L. (a) Derive the marginal cost of labour and find the employment and wage the monopsonist chooses. (b) Find the competitive employment and wage. (c) Find employment if a minimum wage is set at (i) £15, (ii) £18 and (iii) £20. (d) 'Minimum wages always destroy jobs.' Using your results and empirical evidence, evaluate this claim.
markScheme: Total labour cost = wL = 5L + 0.5L², so the marginal cost of labour = 5 + L
Setting MCL = MRP: 5 + L = 25 − 0.5L, so L ≈ 13.3 and the wage is read off supply: w = 5 + 6.67 ≈ £11.67, below the MRP of about £18.33
Competitive outcome: 5 + 0.5L = 25 − 0.5L, so L = 20 and w = £15
Minimum wage £15: the marginal cost of labour is flat at 15 up to L = 20, so L = 20 (employment rises)
£18: employment where MRP = 18, so L = 14, still above the monopsony level, though 2,600 workers (L = 26) would like to work
£20: L = 10, below the monopsony level, so jobs are lost; the threshold is a wage of about £18.33
Evidence: Card and Krueger (1994) found no employment loss after New Jersey's rise; much UK research has found small or no employment effects at the levels the National Minimum Wage has been set

Counter-evidence and caveats: effects depend on the bite (minimum relative to median wage), on hours, prices and profits, and on monopsony power; the competitive model applies where labour markets are thick
Links to efficiency wage and labour discipline arguments; distributional benefits
Balanced conclusion and structure
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) To hire one more worker, the monopsonist must raise the wage for everyone. Total cost is wL = 5L + 0.5L², so the marginal cost of labour is 5 + L, which lies above the supply curve. Setting it equal to MRP: 5 + L = 25 − 0.5L, so L = 13.33 (about 1,333 workers). The firm pays only what is needed to attract them: w = 5 + 0.5 × 13.33 ≈ £11.67, well below the MRP of about £18.33.

(b) In a competitive market, supply equals MRP: 5 + 0.5L = 25 − 0.5L, so L = 20 and w = £15.

(c) (i) At £15 the firm can hire anyone up to 20 at that wage, so its marginal cost of labour is £15 and it hires until MRP = 15: L = 20. Both employment and wages rise. (ii) At £18, 2,600 workers (L = 26) would like to work, but the firm hires until MRP = 18: L = 14, still above the monopsony level. (iii) At £20, L = 10, below 13.33, so the minimum wage now costs jobs. Employment exceeds the monopsony level for any minimum wage up to about £18.33.

(d) The claim follows from the competitive model, where a binding floor raises the wage above the market-clearing level and reduces labour demanded. Under monopsony, a moderate minimum can raise both pay and employment, as shown. Only a high minimum destroys jobs. Card and Krueger (1994) found no fall in fast-food employment in New Jersey after its minimum wage rose, relative to Pennsylvania. Much UK research has found small or no employment effects at the levels the National Minimum Wage has been set. Firms may respond in other ways: raising prices, accepting lower profits, cutting hours, or benefiting from lower turnover and higher effort, as efficiency wage and labour discipline models suggest.

The effect depends on the bite: a minimum close to the median wage, or in low-wage regions, is more likely to reduce employment. Evidence from one level of minimum wage does not guarantee the same result at higher levels.

Conclusion: 'always' is false. The employment effect depends on market structure and on how high the floor is set relative to productivity.

questions.q: Douglass North famously described institutions as:
options: Organisations such as firms, banks and universities
The rules of the game in a society
questions.why: North defined institutions as the formal and informal rules that constrain interaction. Organisations such as firms are the players operating under those rules.

questions.q: In 'The Colonial Origins of Comparative Development' (2001), Acemoglu, Johnson and Robinson identified the effect of institutions on income using which instrument?
options: Mortality rates faced by early European settlers
The legal origin of each country (common vs civil law)
questions.why: They argued that settler mortality shaped whether Europeans settled and built protective institutions, which in turn affect income today. Population density in 1500 was used in their related 'reversal of fortune' work.

questions.q: Explain why secure property rights are thought to promote investment and growth, and give one limitation of this argument.
markScheme: Secure rights let owners capture the returns from investment, which raises the incentive to invest
They reduce resources wasted on defending assets and allow trade and specialisation
They enable assets to be used as collateral, improving access to credit
Limitation: e.g. property rights can entrench existing inequalities, titling may not improve credit access in practice, or rights protecting incumbents can block innovation
questions.modelAnswer: If people expect to keep the returns from their investments, they are more willing to invest in land, buildings, machinery and skills. Secure rights also cut the resources spent guarding assets, make trade and specialisation safer, and let assets serve as collateral for loans. A limitation is that rights protecting existing holders can entrench inequality or block new entrants: the question is whose rights are protected. Evidence also suggests that formal land titles do not always improve access to credit if banks remain unwilling to lend to the poor.

questions.q: Smoke from a factory damages a neighbouring laundry, causing £300 a week of damage. A filter that eliminates the smoke costs the factory £200 a week. Assume bargaining is costless. Using the Coase theorem, explain the outcome (a) if the laundry has the right to clean air, and (b) if the factory has the right to pollute. Then explain why the theorem may fail in practice.
markScheme: Efficient outcome: install the filter, since £200 < £300 of damage
(a) Laundry has the right: the factory installs the filter (cheaper than £300 compensation)
(b) Factory has the right: the laundry pays the factory between £200 and £300 a week to install the filter
Same efficient outcome, but different distribution of gains: the assignment of rights determines who pays
Failure: transaction costs, many affected parties and free riding, asymmetric information about costs, or wealth constraints on the payer
questions.modelAnswer: Installing the filter is efficient because it costs £200 and prevents £300 of damage. (a) If the laundry has the right to clean air, the factory must stop polluting or compensate the laundry £300. It chooses the £200 filter. (b) If the factory may pollute, the laundry gains by paying it between £200 and £300 a week to install the filter. Either way the filter is installed, but who bears the cost depends on the assignment of rights. In practice, bargaining fails when transaction costs are high, when many victims face free-rider problems, when costs are private information, or when victims cannot afford to pay.

questions.q: In the fictional country of Veridia, many rural households farm land they have occupied for decades without formal legal title. Disputes are settled by village elders, and occasionally officials or powerful landlords seize plots. The government proposes a nationwide programme to give these households formal, registered land titles. (a) Using economic reasoning about property rights and institutions, explain the effects you would expect the programme to have on investment, credit and labour allocation. (b) Discuss reasons why the programme might fail to deliver these benefits. (c) Explain how economists could rigorously evaluate the programme's effects.
markScheme: Security of tenure raises the expected return to long-term investment (irrigation, soil improvement, housing)
Less time spent guarding land frees labour for work elsewhere or for schooling
Titles may serve as collateral and increase access to credit (de Soto's argument)
Evidence: Galiani and Schargrodsky (2010) in Buenos Aires found titled households invested more in their housing but saw little gain in credit access
Possible failures: banks unwilling to lend to small farmers, costly foreclosure, weak courts and registry corruption
Formal titling may override customary rights, disadvantaging women or secondary users, and may let elites capture land
Evaluation design: randomised phase-in, or difference-in-differences comparing early and late regions, with attention to selection bias
A clear structure and a conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Insecure tenure acts like a tax on investment: a household that builds irrigation or improves soil may lose the plot before reaping the gains. Secure titles raise the expected return on long-lived investments, so investment in land and housing should rise. Households currently guard their plots by keeping someone at home. With titles, labour is freed for off-farm jobs or schooling. De Soto argued that formal titles turn 'dead capital' into collateral, giving households access to credit to finance investment.

(b) The benefits depend on complementary institutions. Banks may still refuse small loans because transaction costs are high, rural incomes risky, or repossession politically or legally difficult, so collateral value may be limited. If courts and registries are corrupt, a paper title gives little protection against powerful landlords. Formalisation can also override customary arrangements: titles registered to male household heads may weaken women's claims, and well-connected elites may manipulate the registration process to acquire land. Distribution and power, not just the existence of rights, shape outcomes.

(c) Simply comparing titled and untitled households is misleading, because those who obtain titles may be richer or better connected. Credible evaluation needs a comparison group that differs only in receiving a title. The government could phase the programme in randomly across districts, making it a randomised controlled trial, or use difference-in-differences, comparing changes in outcomes in early and late regions before and after titling. Natural experiments help too: Galiani and Schargrodsky (2010) studied Buenos Aires squatters, some of whom did not receive titles only because the former owners challenged the expropriation in court, for reasons unrelated to the households' characteristics. They found titled families invested more in their homes but saw little improvement in access to credit.

Conclusion: titling is likely to increase investment through security of tenure, but its credit effects are uncertain and its distributional consequences need careful design.

questions.q: 'Institutions, rather than geography or culture, are the fundamental cause of differences in prosperity across countries.' Discuss.
markScheme: Distinguishes proximate causes (capital, technology, skills) from fundamental causes (institutions, geography, culture)
Institutions argument: inclusive vs extractive institutions; North's rules of the game
Evidence: AJR (2001) settler mortality instrument; the Korean natural experiment; reversal of fortune
Credible commitment and historical cases such as the Glorious Revolution (North and Weingast)
Geography: disease burden, agricultural productivity, access to the sea and trade; Sachs-style critiques of AJR
Culture: trust, norms and values; evidence that norms persist and affect cooperation
Interactions: geography shaped institutions (e.g. via settler mortality); institutions shape culture and vice versa
Methodological evaluation: endogeneity, validity of instruments, data quality and the risk of 'institutions' becoming a catch-all
Recognises that the same formal institutions work differently in different contexts
Well-structured argument with a justified conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
Capital, technology and skills are proximate causes of prosperity. The question is why some societies accumulate them and others do not. Three fundamental explanations compete: institutions, geography and culture.

The institutional view holds that the 'rules of the game' determine incentives. Inclusive institutions, with secure property rights, constraints on rulers and broad participation, encourage investment and innovation. Extractive institutions channel rents to elites and deter both. The two Koreas are a striking natural experiment: similar geography and culture before 1945, then radically different institutions and hugely divergent living standards. Acemoglu, Johnson and Robinson (2001) used settler mortality to isolate exogenous variation in colonial institutions and found large effects on income today. Their 'reversal of fortune' work notes that colonies that were relatively prosperous in 1500 became poorer, which is hard to explain by fixed geography. North and Weingast argued that the constraints placed on the English Crown after 1688 made its debt promises credible and supported financial development.

Geography still matters. Disease burdens, tropical soils and landlocked locations raise the costs of production and trade, and critics argue that settler mortality may affect income directly through disease, not only through institutions, which would violate the instrument's validity. Geography also shaped institutions: where Europeans could not survive, they set up extractive colonies. Culture matters too: levels of trust and norms of cooperation differ persistently, affect how contracts and public goods function, and may be shaped by institutions in turn.

The explanations therefore interact rather than compete. The same formal rules can work very differently where informal norms differ, as attempts to transplant institutions show. Methodologically, institutions are hard to measure and are themselves endogenous to income, and the label can become a catch-all for anything that explains the residual.

Conclusion: the evidence makes a strong case that institutions are the most important fundamental cause, particularly for explaining why neighbouring societies diverge. But geography and culture help determine which institutions emerge and how they function, so 'rather than' overstates the case. 'Mainly through' would be more defensible.

questions.q: A public good is one that is:
questions.why: Public goods are defined by non-rivalry and non-excludability, not by who provides them. Rival but non-excludable goods are common-pool resources.

questions.q: In Akerlof's 'market for lemons', what happens when buyers cannot observe the quality of used cars but sellers can?
options: Prices rise to reflect average quality, attracting more high-quality sellers
Owners of high-quality cars withdraw because the price reflects average quality, so average quality falls and the market may unravel
Sellers offer warranties, so the market reaches the full-information outcome automatically
Buyers pay more for cars than they are worth, creating excess supply of high-quality cars
questions.why: This is adverse selection: hidden quality drives good cars out, lowering the average quality and price further. Warranties can help, but they are a remedy, not an automatic outcome.

questions.q: Distinguish adverse selection from moral hazard, using health insurance as an example, and suggest a remedy for each.
markScheme: Adverse selection: hidden characteristics before the contract, e.g. people with higher health risks are more likely to buy insurance
This can raise premiums and drive out low-risk buyers (a death spiral)
Moral hazard: hidden actions after the contract, e.g. insured people take less care or use more treatment
Remedies: compulsory or universal insurance and risk pooling for adverse selection; co-payments, deductibles or monitoring for moral hazard
questions.modelAnswer: Adverse selection concerns hidden characteristics before a contract. People who know they are at high risk are keener to buy health insurance. Premiums based on average risk then rise, healthy people drop out, and the market can spiral towards collapse. Compulsory or universal coverage, as with a tax-funded health service, pools risks and prevents this. Moral hazard concerns hidden actions after the contract. Once insured, people may take fewer precautions or use more care than they would if paying the full cost. Co-payments, deductibles and monitoring give the insured some stake in costs.

questions.q: In a competitive market, demand is P = 50 − Q and private marginal cost is MPC = 10 + Q. Production causes a constant marginal external cost of £6 per unit. Find the market outcome, the socially efficient outcome, the Pigouvian tax and the deadweight loss of the unregulated market.
markScheme: Market: 50 − Q = 10 + Q, so Q = 20 and P = £30
Social marginal cost = 16 + Q; efficient outcome: 50 − Q = 16 + Q, so Q = 17 and P = £33
Pigouvian tax = £6 per unit (the marginal external cost at the optimum)
Deadweight loss = ½ × 6 × (20 − 17) = £9
Interpretation: the market overproduces because producers ignore the external cost
questions.modelAnswer: Unregulated, the market sets demand equal to private marginal cost: 50 − Q = 10 + Q, so Q = 20 and P = £30. Social marginal cost is 10 + Q + 6 = 16 + Q, so the efficient output satisfies 50 − Q = 16 + Q, giving Q = 17 and P = £33. A Pigouvian tax of £6 per unit makes producers face the full social cost and delivers this outcome. The three extra units produced in the free market cost society more than buyers value them, giving a deadweight loss of ½ × 6 × 3 = £9.

questions.q: Two firms, Ashby and Brook, each emit 50 tonnes of a pollutant. The regulator wants to cut total emissions by 60 tonnes. Ashby's marginal abatement cost is MACA = 2a and Brook's is MACB = 4b, where a and b are the tonnes each firm abates. (a) Calculate the total abatement cost if each firm must cut emissions by 30 tonnes (a uniform standard). (b) Find the cost-minimising allocation of abatement and its total cost. (c) Show that a tax of £80 per tonne achieves the cost-minimising allocation. (d) Show how a tradable permit scheme issuing 20 permits (each allowing one tonne) to each firm can reach the same outcome, and calculate each firm's gain from trade. (e) Evaluate taxes versus tradable permits as tools of environmental policy.
markScheme: Uniform standard: Ashby's cost = a² = 900; Brook's = 2b² = 1,800; total £2,700
Cost minimisation requires equal marginal abatement costs: 2a = 4b with a + b = 60, so a = 40 and b = 20
Minimum cost: 1,600 + 800 = £2,400, a saving of £300
Under a £80 tax, each firm abates until MAC = 80: Ashby abates 40 tonnes, Brook 20
Permits: Ashby abates 40 and sells 10 permits to Brook at £80; Brook abates 20
A tax fixes the price and leaves quantity uncertain; permits fix quantity and leave price uncertain (Weitzman, 1974)
Further points: revenue from taxes or auctioned permits, permit price volatility, political economy and free allocation, carbon leakage, monitoring costs
Reasoned conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Abatement cost is the area under each MAC curve: Ashby's cost is a² and Brook's is 2b². Under a uniform 30-tonne cut, Ashby pays 900 and Brook 1,800, a total of £2,700.

(b) Total cost is minimised when the last tonne costs the same at both firms. Otherwise, shifting abatement to the cheaper firm saves money. Setting 2a = 4b with a + b = 60 gives a = 40 and b = 20, with MAC = £80 at both firms. Total cost is 1,600 + 800 = £2,400, saving £300.

(c) With a £80 tax per tonne emitted, each firm abates as long as abating is cheaper than paying the tax, i.e. until MAC = 80. Ashby abates 40 tonnes and Brook 20, the cost-minimising allocation, and the regulator needs no information about individual firms' costs.

(d) With 20 permits each, both firms must initially cut 30 tonnes. Ashby's MAC at 30 tonnes is £60, Brook's £120, so trade is profitable. Ashby abates 10 more tonnes (40 in total) and sells 10 permits to Brook at £80, and Brook abates only 20. Ashby's extra abatement costs 1,600 − 900 = £700 but earns £800: a gain of £100. Brook saves 1,800 − 800 = £1,000 in abatement and pays £800: a gain of £200. The £300 total equals the saving in (b).

(e) With full information, the two instruments are equivalent. Under uncertainty about abatement costs, a tax fixes the price of pollution and leaves the quantity uncertain, while permits fix the quantity and leave the price uncertain. Weitzman (1974) showed that the choice depends on whether the damage from pollution or the abatement cost curve is steeper. Taxes raise revenue automatically, and permits do so if auctioned, but permits are often given away free, which eases political acceptance at the cost of revenue. Permit prices can be volatile, discouraging long-term investment, which has led to price floors and reserves in practice. Both instruments face monitoring costs and the risk of carbon leakage to unregulated jurisdictions.

Conclusion: either market-based instrument beats a uniform standard. For a stock pollutant like carbon, where the damage from each extra tonne changes little, a price-based instrument has strong arguments in its favour.

questions.q: 'Market failure is a necessary but not a sufficient justification for government intervention.' Discuss.
markScheme: Defines market failure as departures from Pareto efficiency: externalities, public goods, asymmetric information, market power
Links to the first welfare theorem and its assumptions
Necessary? Challenges this: intervention may also be justified on grounds of fairness, distribution or merit goods even when markets are efficient
Not sufficient: government failure such as limited information (Hayek), regulatory capture, rent-seeking and political incentives
Private solutions: Coasean bargaining, Ostrom's community governance, reputation and warranties
Theory of the second best: correcting one distortion may not raise welfare
Costs of intervention: administration, the deadweight loss of taxation, unintended consequences
Comparative institutional analysis: compare imperfect markets with imperfect governments
Examples (e.g. climate change, healthcare, natural monopoly regulation) to support the argument
Structured evaluation and a conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
Market failure occurs when market outcomes are not Pareto efficient: because of externalities, public goods, asymmetric information or market power, the assumptions of the first welfare theorem fail. The proposition makes two claims, and both deserve scrutiny.

Is market failure necessary? Arguably not. Efficiency is only one criterion. A perfectly competitive market can produce a Pareto-efficient outcome in which some people cannot afford food or healthcare, and governments routinely intervene for distributional or fairness reasons through taxes and transfers. Merit goods such as schooling may be supported because society values them independently of individual preferences. So market failure is one justification among several, not a precondition. The proposition is more defensible if it is limited to efficiency-based arguments.

Is it sufficient? Here the proposition is strong. Governments face their own information problems. Hayek emphasised that prices aggregate dispersed knowledge no planner can collect, and a regulator setting a Pigouvian tax must estimate external costs. Public choice theory points to regulatory capture, rent-seeking by interest groups and electoral short-termism. Interventions have administrative costs and are funded by distortionary taxation. The theory of the second best warns that fixing one distortion while others remain does not guarantee a welfare gain.

Private or community alternatives may also solve the problem. Coase showed that with clear rights and low transaction costs, bargaining can internalise externalities. Ostrom documented communities governing commons through their own rules. Warranties and reputation can mitigate asymmetric information in used-car markets.

The right test is comparative: is the imperfect market outcome worse than the likely imperfect government outcome? For climate change, the externality is global, large and involves millions of parties, so Coasean bargaining is impossible and intervention through carbon pricing is strongly justified despite the risk of government failure. For a minor local externality, the costs of regulation may exceed the gains.

Conclusion: market failure is not strictly necessary, since equity can justify intervention, and it is certainly not sufficient. It establishes a case for considering intervention, which must then be weighed against the probability and costs of government failure.

questions.q: Which component of aggregate demand is typically the most volatile over the business cycle in advanced economies?
questions.why: Investment depends on expectations of future demand and profits and can easily be postponed, so it swings far more than consumption, which households try to smooth.

questions.q: In a closed economy with no taxes and a marginal propensity to consume of 0.75, autonomous investment falls by £20bn. By how much does equilibrium output fall?
questions.why: The multiplier is 1/(1 − 0.75) = 4, so output falls by 4 × £20bn = £80bn as lost income reduces consumption in successive rounds.

questions.q: Explain the permanent income hypothesis and give two reasons why households may not smooth consumption as it predicts.
markScheme: Consumption depends on expected lifetime (permanent) income, not current income
Temporary income changes have little effect on consumption; permanent changes have large effects
Reason 1: credit constraints prevent borrowing against future income
Reason 2: weakness of will/present bias, or precautionary saving under uncertainty, or limited information
questions.modelAnswer: The permanent income hypothesis says households base consumption on their expected long-run income. A temporary windfall or loss is spread across many years, so it barely changes current spending, while a permanent change in income changes consumption almost one-for-one. In practice households often respond strongly to temporary changes. Many face credit constraints: banks will not lend against uncertain future earnings, so a temporary income fall forces spending cuts. Others show present bias or weakness of will and spend windfalls quickly. Uncertainty also prompts precautionary saving, especially in recessions.

questions.q: A bank's balance sheet is: assets of £500bn (loans £400bn; reserves and government bonds £100bn); liabilities of deposits £400bn and short-term wholesale borrowing £75bn; equity £25bn. (a) Calculate the bank's leverage ratio. (b) If 5% of its loans default with no recovery, calculate the new equity and leverage. (c) What percentage of loans must be lost to make the bank insolvent? (d) Explain why high leverage made the 2008 financial crisis so damaging.
markScheme: Leverage = assets/equity = 500/25 = 20
Loan losses = 5% × 400 = £20bn; equity falls to £5bn
New assets £480bn, so leverage = 480/5 = 96
Insolvency when losses exceed £25bn = 6.25% of loans (5% of total assets)
High leverage means small asset losses wipe out equity, triggering fire sales and a loss of funding (especially short-term wholesale funding)
Banks cut lending to rebuild capital, causing a credit crunch that spread to the real economy; hence higher capital requirements after the crisis
questions.modelAnswer: Leverage is 500/25 = 20. A 5% default on loans costs £20bn, cutting equity to £5bn while assets fall to £480bn, so leverage jumps to 96. Losses of £25bn, 6.25% of loans, would make the bank insolvent. Before 2008, many banks were highly leveraged and relied on short-term wholesale funding. Modest falls in asset values, such as mortgage-backed securities, threatened their solvency. Lenders withdrew funding, banks sold assets in fire sales, which pushed prices down further, and cut lending to rebuild capital ratios. The resulting credit crunch hit household and business spending, which is why regulators now require larger capital buffers.

questions.q: In a closed economy, consumption is C = 50 + 0.75(Y − T), government spending is G = 150, lump-sum taxes are T = 100, and investment depends on output: I = 10 + 0.1Y. (a) Find equilibrium output, consumption, investment and private saving. (b) Households become more pessimistic and autonomous consumption falls from 50 to 30 as they try to save more. Find the new equilibrium output and private saving. (c) Repeat (b) assuming instead that investment is fixed at 100 regardless of output. (d) Use your results to explain the paradox of thrift, and evaluate its relevance during a recession.
markScheme: C = 650, I = 100, disposable income 800, private saving = 800 − 650 = 150
New output: Y = 115/0.15 ≈ 766.7; C = 530, I ≈ 86.7; saving ≈ 136.7, which is lower than before
Fixed investment: Y = 205/0.25 = 820; saving = 720 − 570 = 150, unchanged
Explanation: in a closed economy S + T = I + G, so saving cannot rise unless investment (or the budget balance) changes
When investment responds to output, attempts to save more reduce total saving
Evaluation: relevance is greatest in recessions and at the lower bound; in normal times interest rates can fall and stimulate investment, and in an open economy net exports adjust
Policy implication: the case for fiscal support when private saving rises
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Y = C + I + G = 50 + 0.75(Y − 100) + 10 + 0.1Y + 150 = 135 + 0.85Y, so 0.15Y = 135 and Y = 900. Then C = 50 + 0.75 × 800 = 650, I = 10 + 90 = 100, and private saving = Y − T − C = 800 − 650 = 150. The multiplier is 1/(1 − 0.75 − 0.1) ≈ 6.67, larger than usual because investment rises with output.

(b) With autonomous consumption of 30, Y = 115 + 0.85Y, so Y = 115/0.15 ≈ 766.7. Disposable income is 666.7, C = 30 + 0.75 × 666.7 = 530, I = 10 + 76.7 = 86.7, and saving = 666.7 − 530 ≈ 136.7. Households tried to save 20 more at the original income, but saving actually falls by about 13, and output falls by about 133.

(c) With I fixed at 100, Y = 30 − 75 + 100 + 150 + 0.75Y, so 0.25Y = 205 and Y = 820. C = 30 + 0.75 × 720 = 570 and saving = 720 − 570 = 150, exactly unchanged.

(d) In a closed economy, national income accounting gives S + T = I + G. If investment and the budget are fixed, private saving cannot change however hard households try: their reduced spending lowers others' incomes until saving returns to its original level. If investment responds positively to output, as firms cut investment when sales fall, total saving falls. This is the paradox of thrift: behaviour that is prudent for one household is self-defeating for all households together.

The paradox is most relevant in a recession, when many households increase precautionary saving simultaneously and firms cut investment. It is especially strong when the central bank cannot cut interest rates further, as at the lower bound after 2008. In normal times, falling demand would prompt rate cuts that stimulate investment, absorbing extra saving. In an open economy, part of the adjustment comes through net exports. The paradox provides a key argument for fiscal expansion when private demand collapses.

questions.q: In the fictional economy of Freedonia, statisticians estimate the following Okun relationship: Δu = −0.4(g − 2.5), where Δu is the annual change in the unemployment rate (percentage points) and g is annual real GDP growth (%). (a) Calculate the change in unemployment if GDP contracts by 2% in a recession year. (b) What growth rate would be needed to reduce unemployment by 1 percentage point in a year? (c) Interpret the 2.5 and the 0.4 in the equation and explain why the coefficient on output is less than one. (d) Explain how household and firm behaviour can amplify a downturn once unemployment starts to rise.
markScheme: g = −2: Δu = −0.4 × (−4.5) = +1.8 percentage points
2.5 is roughly trend growth (from productivity and labour force growth) needed to keep unemployment constant
The 0.4 coefficient: output changes are only partly reflected in unemployment
Reasons: labour hoarding, changes in hours, participation changes and procyclical productivity
Amplification: precautionary saving and lower consumption by households fearing job loss
Firms cut investment as expected demand falls (accelerator effect, animal spirits)
Credit constraints tighten in downturns; the multiplier spreads the initial fall in spending
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) With g = −2, Δu = −0.4 × (−2 − 2.5) = −0.4 × (−4.5) = +1.8 percentage points.

(b) To cut unemployment by 1 point, −1 = −0.4(g − 2.5), so g − 2.5 = 2.5 and g = 5%. Freedonia must grow well above trend to bring unemployment down.

(c) The 2.5 is approximately trend growth: the growth rate at which unemployment is stable, determined by productivity growth and labour force growth. Growth below this means demand for labour rises more slowly than supply plus productivity, so unemployment rises. The 0.4 indicates that a 1% shortfall of output below trend raises unemployment by only 0.4 points. Firms hoard labour in downturns, keeping skilled staff and cutting hours rather than jobs, because hiring and training are costly. Some people who lose jobs leave the labour force instead of being counted as unemployed. Productivity also tends to fall in recessions as workers are under-used.

(d) Once unemployment rises, the downturn can feed on itself. Households facing a higher risk of job loss build up precautionary savings and postpone large purchases, especially if they cannot borrow, which lowers consumption. Lower sales reduce firms' expected profits, and because investment depends on expected future demand, it falls sharply. Pessimism, Keynes's animal spirits, can spread. Banks become more cautious and tighten credit just when households and firms need it. Each cut in spending reduces someone else's income, so the multiplier magnifies the initial shock. Automatic stabilisers such as unemployment benefits and falling tax revenues partly offset this, which is one reason output volatility is lower in economies with larger welfare states.

The Okun relationship is a stylised regularity, not a structural law: its coefficients vary across countries and over time with labour market institutions.

questions.q: 'Recessions that follow financial crises are deeper and longer than ordinary recessions because of what happens to the balance sheets of households and banks.' Discuss, with reference to the Great Depression and the 2008 global financial crisis.
markScheme: Stylised fact: post-crisis recessions tend to be deeper with slower recoveries (Reinhart and Rogoff, 2009)
Household balance sheets: leverage, falling house prices, negative equity and deleveraging reduce consumption (Mian and Sufi)
Precautionary saving and the paradox of thrift deepen the fall in demand
Bank balance sheets: high leverage, losses on assets, loss of funding and fire sales
The credit crunch reduces lending to firms and households and hits investment
Debt deflation (Fisher): falling prices raise real debt burdens, as in the Great Depression
Great Depression: bank failures, deflation and contractionary policy errors (gold standard)
2008: rapid policy response (rate cuts, QE, fiscal stimulus, bank recapitalisation) prevented deflation and collapse of the banking system, though the recovery was slow
Evaluation: the role of policy alongside balance sheets; alternative explanations (supply-side damage, hysteresis, austerity)
Coherent structure and a conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
Reinhart and Rogoff's (2009) historical survey found that recessions following banking crises tend to involve larger output falls and slower recoveries than ordinary recessions. The proposition attributes this to balance sheets. That is a large part of the story, but policy also matters.

Household balance sheets: in the run-up to 2008, households in the US, the UK and elsewhere borrowed heavily against rising house prices. When prices fell, many households saw their equity shrink or turn negative. Mian and Sufi showed that US areas with higher household leverage experienced larger falls in consumption. Indebted households cut spending to repair their balance sheets. Combined with precautionary saving driven by unemployment risk, this produced a large, persistent fall in demand. The paradox of thrift means such deleveraging lowers income for everyone.

Bank balance sheets: banks were highly leveraged, so modest losses on mortgage-related assets threatened solvency. Short-term wholesale funding dried up, forcing fire sales that depressed asset prices further. To rebuild capital, banks cut lending, creating a credit crunch that hit firms' investment even where demand was sound. Ordinary recessions do not usually damage the financial system's ability to lend.

The Great Depression adds debt deflation. As thousands of US banks failed and the money supply contracted, prices fell sharply, raising the real burden of debt, as Fisher (1933) described. Policy aggravated this: adherence to the gold standard led to tight monetary policy, and governments tried to balance budgets.

In 2008, policymakers drew lessons from the 1930s. They cut interest rates to near zero, introduced quantitative easing, recapitalised banks and allowed large fiscal deficits. Deflation and a banking collapse were avoided, but the recovery was still slow. This is consistent with balance-sheet repair taking years, though the shift to fiscal austerity in some countries after 2010 and persistent weakness in productivity growth are alternative or complementary explanations.

Conclusion: balance sheets explain why financial crises cause unusually large, persistent falls in demand and credit. The contrast between the 1930s and 2008 shows that policy responses determine how deep and long the downturn becomes.

questions.q: What inflation target is the Bank of England's Monetary Policy Committee required to meet?
questions.why: The Chancellor sets a target of 2% for consumer price index (CPI) inflation. The earlier target of 2.5% applied to RPIX.

questions.q: A central bank follows the Taylor rule i = r* + π + 0.5(π − π*) + 0.5(output gap), with neutral real rate r* = 2%, inflation π = 4%, target π* = 2% and an output gap of −1%. What policy rate does the rule prescribe?
questions.why: i = 2 + 4 + 0.5(2) + 0.5(−1) = 6.5%. The real policy rate is 2.5%, above neutral, because inflation is above target.

questions.q: Explain why making the central bank independent may lead to lower inflation, using the idea of time inconsistency.
markScheme: Governments may promise low inflation but have an incentive, once expectations are set, to create surprise inflation to boost output (e.g. before elections)
Rational wage-setters anticipate this, so expected inflation rises: an inflation bias with no output gain (Kydland and Prescott, 1977; Barro and Gordon)
An independent central bank with a clear mandate (and possibly conservative preferences) can credibly commit to low inflation
Credibility anchors expectations, lowering inflation at lower output cost; caveat: democratic accountability or coordination with fiscal policy
questions.modelAnswer: A government may announce low inflation, but once wages and prices are set it is tempted to stimulate the economy with surprise inflation to cut unemployment, especially before elections. Wage-setters anticipate this temptation and build higher expected inflation into their bargains, so the economy ends up with higher inflation and no lasting output gain. This is the inflation bias identified by Kydland and Prescott (1977). Delegating policy to an independent central bank with a clear inflation mandate removes the short-term political incentive and makes the low-inflation promise credible. Expectations stay anchored, so disinflation is cheaper. The trade-off is reduced democratic control.

questions.q: (a) The nominal interest rate on a one-year deposit is 5% and expected inflation is 3%. Estimate the real interest rate approximately and exactly. (b) A perpetual bond pays £5 a year. Calculate its price when the market interest rate is 5% and when it falls to 4%, and explain the relationship.
markScheme: Approximate real rate ≈ 5 − 3 = 2%
Exact real rate = 1.05/1.03 − 1 ≈ 1.94%
Bond price = 5/0.05 = £100, rising to 5/0.04 = £125
Prices and yields move inversely: the fixed coupon must give the new, lower market yield, so the price rises
questions.modelAnswer: By the Fisher equation, the real rate is approximately 5% − 3% = 2%. Exactly, (1.05/1.03) − 1 ≈ 1.94%. A perpetuity's price equals its coupon divided by the interest rate: £5/0.05 = £100 at 5%, and £5/0.04 = £125 at 4%. Because the coupon is fixed, the bond's price must rise until its yield matches the new, lower market rate. This inverse relationship is why central bank purchases of bonds (QE), which push up prices, lower long-term interest rates.

questions.q: A closed economy is described by C = 50 + 0.75(Y − T), I = 100, G = 150 and lump-sum taxes T = 100. (a) Calculate equilibrium output and the budget balance. (b) Calculate the government spending multiplier, the tax multiplier and the balanced budget multiplier. (c) Output consistent with full employment is 1,000. Calculate the change in G alone, the change in T alone, and the equal change in G and T that would close the gap, and the budget balance in each case. (d) Evaluate which option the government should choose, and why the real-world multiplier might differ from your calculation.
markScheme: Budget balance T − G = −50 (deficit of 50)
Spending multiplier 1/(1 − 0.75) = 4; tax multiplier −0.75/0.25 = −3; balanced budget multiplier 1
To close the gap of 100: ΔG = +25 (deficit 75); ΔT = −33.3 (deficit 83.3); ΔG = ΔT = +100 (deficit unchanged at 50)
Spending is more powerful per pound because part of a tax cut is saved
Real multipliers are smaller with proportional taxes, imports and crowding out, and with Ricardian or forward-looking behaviour
Multipliers are larger in deep recessions and at the lower bound, and with credit-constrained households
Considerations: debt levels, time lags, composition (investment vs transfers), and a reasoned choice
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Y = 50 + 0.75(Y − 100) + 100 + 150 = 225 + 0.75Y, so 0.25Y = 225 and Y = 900. With G = 150 and T = 100, the government runs a deficit of 50.

(b) The spending multiplier is 1/(1 − 0.75) = 4. A tax cut first raises disposable income, of which only 75% is spent, so the tax multiplier is −0.75/0.25 = −3. Raising G and T together by the same amount gives 4 − 3 = 1: the balanced budget multiplier.

(c) The gap is 100. Raising G by 25 closes it, increasing the deficit to 75. Cutting taxes alone requires ΔT = −100/3 ≈ −33.3, raising the deficit to about 83.3. A balanced expansion requires G and T both to rise by 100, leaving the deficit at 50 but enlarging the state considerably.

(d) Spending is the most 'efficient' option per pound of extra deficit, because none of the first-round injection leaks into saving. The tax cut leaves more choice with households but costs more. The balanced budget route avoids higher borrowing but requires large tax increases, which may be politically difficult and could damage incentives.

Real-world multipliers differ from this model. Proportional income taxes and imports create leakages that reduce the multiplier. Higher borrowing may raise interest rates and crowd out investment, unless the central bank holds rates down or rates are at the lower bound. Forward-looking households may save part of a temporary tax cut in anticipation of future taxes, in the Ricardian spirit, though credit-constrained households will spend more. Evidence suggests multipliers are larger in deep recessions and when monetary policy is constrained, and IMF analysis by Blanchard and Leigh (2013) found forecasters had underestimated multipliers during the post-2010 fiscal consolidations.

In a recession with interest rates near zero and high unemployment, temporary public investment is probably the best choice: it has a high multiplier and also raises long-run capacity. If debt is already high, the government should weigh the cost of extra borrowing against the costs of persistent unemployment.

questions.q: The government of Aldoria has debt of 100% of GDP. The average nominal interest rate on its debt is 4%, nominal GDP growth is 2%, and it runs a primary deficit (spending excluding interest minus revenue) of 1% of GDP. Debt evolves according to d(t+1) = d(t)(1 + r)/(1 + g) − pb, where pb is the primary balance as a share of GDP. (a) Calculate the debt ratio after one year. (b) Calculate the primary balance needed to stabilise the debt ratio at 100%. (c) The central bank cuts rates and the effective interest rate falls to 1%, with growth unchanged. Recalculate (a) and (b). (d) Using your results, evaluate the argument that Aldoria should pursue immediate fiscal austerity to reduce its debt.
markScheme: Stabilising primary balance: pb = d(r − g)/(1 + g) = 0.02/1.02 ≈ +1.96% of GDP (a surplus)
Stabilising pb = (0.01 − 0.02)/1.02 ≈ −0.98%: a primary deficit of about 1% of GDP is sustainable
Interpretation: the gap between r and g is central to debt dynamics
Austerity reduces the primary deficit but lowers g through the multiplier, possibly raising the debt ratio in the short run if multipliers are large
Hysteresis: prolonged weak demand can permanently reduce output
Counter-argument: high debt raises the risk of rising interest rates and losing market confidence; fiscal space is needed for future shocks
Timing: gradual consolidation once recovery is secured; composition (protecting public investment)
Reasoned conclusion recognising monetary–fiscal interaction
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) d' = 1.00 × 1.04/1.02 + 0.01 = 1.0196 + 0.01 ≈ 1.030, so debt rises to about 103% of GDP. Two forces push it up: interest exceeds growth, and the government borrows to fund a primary deficit.

(b) Stability requires d = d(1 + r)/(1 + g) − pb, so pb = d(r − g)/(1 + g) = 0.02/1.02 ≈ 1.96% of GDP. Aldoria would need to move from a 1% primary deficit to a surplus of about 2%: a fiscal tightening of roughly 3% of GDP.

(c) With r = 1%: d' = 1.01/1.02 + 0.01 = 0.9902 + 0.01 ≈ 1.000, so debt is essentially stable. The stabilising balance becomes pb = (0.01 − 0.02)/1.02 ≈ −0.98%. With r below g, the government can run a primary deficit of about 1% of GDP indefinitely without the debt ratio rising.

(d) The calculations show that debt sustainability depends heavily on r − g, not just on the deficit. Austerity attacks the primary balance, but it also affects g. If the fiscal multiplier is large, as is more likely when the economy is weak and interest rates are already low, cutting spending by 3% of GDP could cut output enough to reduce nominal growth substantially. The debt ratio might then fall little, or even rise in the short run, because GDP is the denominator. Prolonged weak demand can also cause hysteresis: lost skills and investment that permanently reduce output and future tax revenue.

There are counter-arguments. If markets doubt Aldoria's commitment, interest rates could rise sharply, turning r − g strongly positive and making debt explosive. High debt also leaves less room to respond to future shocks. A credible medium-term plan, gradual consolidation once recovery is secure, and protection of productive public investment address both concerns. The interaction with monetary policy is crucial: as part (c) shows, low interest rates sharply ease the fiscal arithmetic, but a central bank targeting inflation cannot be relied on to keep rates low indefinitely.

Conclusion: immediate, front-loaded austerity is hard to justify when r is below g and the economy is weak. A credible plan to stabilise debt over the medium term is the better approach.

questions.q: 'Stabilising the economy is a job for the central bank; fiscal policy should focus on long-term goals and leave short-run demand management alone.' Discuss, with reference to economic experience since the 1990s.
markScheme: The case for monetary dominance: inflation targeting, independence and credibility; fiscal lags and political bias
Evidence: the Great Moderation under inflation targeting (though good luck also played a role)
Limits: the zero lower bound after 2008 restricted conventional monetary policy; QE was used but its effects are debated
Fiscal policy is more powerful when interest rates are at the lower bound and multipliers are higher
Automatic stabilisers already provide fiscal stabilisation without discretion
The COVID-19 pandemic (2020): targeted fiscal measures such as the UK's furlough scheme protected incomes and jobs in ways monetary policy could not
Distributional and sectoral targeting are possible only with fiscal tools
Risks of fiscal activism: debt sustainability, deficit bias, poor timing, market reactions
Coordination: monetary and fiscal interaction; post-2021 inflation showed the risks when both are loose and supply shocks hit
Structured evaluation and a conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
From the 1990s until 2008, the dominant view matched the proposition. Monetary policy could be adjusted quickly by technocrats, while discretionary fiscal policy suffered from decision and implementation lags and from political incentives to run deficits. Inflation-targeting central banks with operational independence, such as the Bank of England from 1997, seemed to deliver low, stable inflation and the Great Moderation, though favourable shocks played a part. Fiscal policy was left to automatic stabilisers and long-run aims such as public investment and debt sustainability.

The 2008 crisis exposed the limits of this division. Policy rates hit the effective lower bound, and central banks turned to quantitative easing and forward guidance. These helped, but their transmission to spending was uncertain, and QE raised asset prices, which may have widened wealth inequality. At the lower bound, fiscal multipliers are likely to be larger because extra borrowing does not push up interest rates. Many economists argued that the shift to fiscal consolidation from around 2010 slowed recovery.

The COVID-19 pandemic strengthened the case for fiscal action. The shock was concentrated in particular sectors, and the priority was to preserve firms and jobs during lockdowns. Interest rate cuts could not do this. Targeted fiscal schemes, such as the UK's Coronavirus Job Retention Scheme, kept workers attached to employers and supported incomes.

There are still good reasons for caution about fiscal activism. Debt ratios rose substantially after 2008 and 2020, and rising interest rates make high debt more expensive. Fiscal decisions are prone to deficit bias and poor timing. The inflation surge from 2021 also showed the danger of combined monetary and fiscal stimulus meeting supply shocks, such as energy price spikes and supply-chain disruption: demand management cannot fix supply problems, and too much stimulus adds to inflation.

Conclusion: in normal times the proposition is broadly right. The central bank should lead stabilisation, supported by automatic stabilisers, while discretionary fiscal policy focuses on the long term. But when interest rates are at the lower bound, or shocks are sectoral and severe, fiscal policy has an essential stabilising role. The best framework allows it to act in these circumstances, within a credible medium-term fiscal anchor.
